subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robert
The Address-Mr. Danforth Lafreniere for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to you, to the Deputy Speaker and to the deputy chairman of committees I must confess that after hearing the congratulations and good wishes that have been expressed by the many hon. members who have preceded me, and noting the real sincerity with which they have been given, I can only add that I concur wholeheartedly. I must say that I admired greatly the manner in which the address in reply to the speech from the throne was moved and seconded, and that I am extremely proud indeed to be associated with these hon. members.
I must also say that a number of others who have since participated in this debate have brought honour and distinction to themselves by their efforts, which seemed to me more like addresses of veterans than those of the novices they profess to be. I have followed with keen interest the subject matters dealt with in this debate and have learned a great deal about this Canada of ours from the hon. members who have dealt at length with the constituencies they represent; and I am very relieved that the constituency which I have the honour to represent is not alone in feeling that this twenty-fourth parliament will provide a means of aiding them with respect to some of their difficulties.
The constituency I represent is the county of Kent, which is the most southerly county in the Dominion of Canada. In fact it is further south than two of the great United States cities, namely Boston and Detroit. Kent county is also further south than approximately one-third of the habitable area of the United States, and 700 miles farther south than its counterpart in England. A line drawn through Chatham, our principal city, if continued across the globe would traverse the south of France. Because of the fact that it is bounded by two of the great lakes, St. Clair and Erie, its climate is temperate to the extent that Kent experiences neither extreme northern cold nor extreme southern heat. It is made up of some 580,000 acres of the best of farm land, and because of its unique situation Kent might be termed a working model of Canada, for here we find nearly every industry and field of endeavour to be found anywhere else in our country, though in some instances to a lesser degree. For this reason our problems are numerous and complex, and the speech from the throne has brought a great surge of hope to the people of this great constituency.

I have stated that we in Kent are engaged in many fields of endeavour. May I point out some of these. In respect to agriculture all grains, from wheat, corn, soybeans, oats and barley to flax and sunflowers are grown there. Fruits are grown from apples, peaches and cherries to strawberries and raspberries; we have specialized crops such as sugar beets, canning tomatoes and tobacco. So far as industry is concerned we build everything from cars, truck and plane bodies to steel boats. The livestock men produce cattle, hogs, sheep and fur-bearing animals whose quality is equal to that produced anywhere else in the world. These are not elaborations on my part, but merely statements of fact.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak of some of the industries in my area, and offer some suggestions as to how they may be aided in their endeavours by the deliberations of hon. members of this house. I should like to talk for a moment or two about our fishing industry. Dotted along our long shoreline are numerous small ports from which fishing ships and tugs operate into the lake. These fishing vessels are constructed of steel; they are from about 45 feet to 75 feet in length, and vary in value from $45,000 to $60,000. They have five men in the crew and are diesel powered. One port near my home has 22 of these tugs operating from it, and another has 37.
Located at Wheatley, which is the name of one of these ports, is the largest fresh water fish processing plant in the world, which annually processes around 20 million pounds of fresh water fish. The province of Ontario produced approximately $7 million worth of fresh water fish in 1957, and the sales from Kent county amounted to over $3,500,000, or more than half. This industry in Kent needs help in two directions. There needs to be a well-thought out plan of progressive construction of docking facilities for these boats, which in many instances are using makeshift, homemade wooden structures some of which are dangerous and not practical. Some dredging work must be done to deepen the entrances to the ports. I have seen these boats scraping bottom time and time again in their attempts to land, and in one instance this spring I saw a new modern tug put its engines out of commission in such an attempt. When the size of the industry is measured against the size of the necessary expenditures, I am sure something can be done on their behalf.
The second great need is in the field of research work on behalf of the fish industry in lake Erie. Lake Erie has been very productive, but it may be overlooked because

of this very fact until it is too late and its stock of fish is depleted, as has happened in other great lakes. For example, right now we would like to know why in lake Erie smelts are lying dead on the bottom by the millions and why, too, fish are being netted in quantities that were never found there as recently as 15 years ago.
Mr. Speaker, may I take the liberty of dwelling at some length on the subject of agriculture, our basic industry. As has been pointed out before many of our endeavours have been pioneered in Kent county and are, in fact, crops grown by specialists. Tobacco is grown to a large extent, and I heartily support the views expressed by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Knowles) on behalf of the tobacco growers. Sugar beets are also a specialized crop. This industry brings about $30 million a year to western Ontario alone and means a great deal to the economy of Canada. The industry was practically crucified in 1952 and 1953 when great quantities of Cuban refined sugar were imported into Canada. A continuation of these imports would have curtailed and even stopped the production and refining of sugar beets in western Ontario. At that time, and I say it without hesitation, the industry was saved through the efforts of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) who waged a continuing battle with the then minister of trade and commerce with the result that Cuban refined sugar shipments were finally stopped. We do import some Cuban raw sugar, however.
Last year, within 44 days of the calling of parliament this government placed a support price on sugar beets of 17 per cent sugar content at $13 per ton. This stimulated interest in sugar beet acreage. The sugar beet growers in western Ontario expected that the support price for 1958 would be above the 1957 figure. As a result the growers have planted something in excess of 30,000 acres of sugar beets as against 19,000 acres the previous year. The support price for 1958 should have been announced prior to the planting season, and I contend it should have been above the announced price. I have no hesitation in saying that had the floor price been 100 per cent or more of the ten-year average an additional 10,000 acres of sugar beets would have been planted. This would have been a planting record, and would have meant a great deal to the economy of Canada.
I submit that the farmers in Ontario who suffered many injustices under the Liberal government have now been recognized by our present government. They should be entitled to even greater consideration because of the high cost of production, as many crops
The Address-Mr. Danforth are grown in small acreages, and their particular problems should be studied more carefully by some department of government. I refer in particular to such crops as wheat, soybeans, sugar beets and corn.
Another endeavour pioneered in Kent, one that is comparatively new but of major importance, is the growing and production of hybrid seed corn. The development of the seed for the growing of commercial corn requires the work of skilled agricultural technicians, and we are fortunate in having the very best of these in Kent county. Every time there is an increase in demand of 1,000 bushels of seed corn, one more farm can be placed in the profitable production of this crop.
I am sure hon. members followed with some interest the visit of the Roumanian trade mission to the farms in Kent county, and took note of the remarks made by the Roumanian minister of agriculture. After visiting the major corn seed companies in the United States he said that the field of corn he was then standing in was the best he had ever seen. At that moment he was standing in a 100-acre seed corn plot on the Warwich hybrid farm in Kent county. The result of this has been that Kent county exported seed corn to Roumania that year, and this year the order has been increased to three times that quantity. The truth of the matter is that the amount of single cross and double cross hybrid seed sent to Roumania, developed for use as commercial seed, will seed approximately 1J million acres of corn.
We need help for our corn industry. We have here a crop that produces more grain and fodder per acre than any other crop. We have here facilities to produce the seed in ever-increasing amounts for home consumption and export. We have in the Ottawa, Kemptville, Harrow and Ridgetown experimental stations the men capable of developing strains to push the climatic-restricting boundaries of corn farther and farther back. We have a commercial crop that does not as yet fill our own requirements and which could utilize land and labour going into the production of crops which are in a surplus position. The government could help by putting a reasonable stabilized price on commercial corn and by controlling the importation of corn into Canada, which comes in by the millions of bushels.
The market for our seed corn overseas could also be explored. It offers a great field for expansion, because our greatest competitors there are the seed companies of the United States. The large markets for this seed are in Yugoslavia, Roumania, East Germany
614	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Danforth and Russia. We can compete successfully because our seed is superior in suitability for conditions in those countries. This is due to the fact that the climate there is wet and cool, somewhat similar to ours. For that reason our seed corn is developed for early maturity and for a cool, wet season, as compared with the United States production of seed for later maturity and growth in a hot, dry climate.
This market is available. Kent county has a very small portion of this market, which nevertheless amounts to thousands of bushels, due to the efforts of one man who visited one country at his own expense. Think for a moment of the potential results of a trade mission representing Canada and well qualified for this task visiting markets abroad.
May I now speak for a few moments on the production of livestock. During the war some of the famous Landrace hogs were taken from Denmark to the Jersey islands to avoid falling into enemy hands. From there some of this stock reached the farms of Sir Winston Churchill. These pigs showed such high feed conversion standards and such quality of bacon that Kent county breeders became interested and at a very high cost imported breeding stock into Kent from these farms by way of Scotland. Work has since gone on at a tremendous rate to develop and expand this stock for breeding. Denmark prohibits the export of this stock, which they have developed to a high degree of perfection, and for that reason it is difficult to obtain this stock on any farm. We in Kent county are extremely proud of the work done in this field. Recently 105 of these animals were crated and flown to Roumania, a repeat order of the nine purchased and shipped to that country last year. Other shipments are continually going to the United States.
Similar developments are occurring in other branches of the livestock industry. Last week in Kent the first Angus and Hereford cattle were being assembled to be shipped to Roumania for breeding stock. In poultry, 17,000 baby chicks were going to the same market. Dairy cattle are continually being exported to the United States and some other countries. These shipments are made possible because of the high standard of quality that obtains in Kent county in all these branches of livestock.
My purpose, sir, is twofold. First I wish to point out the fact that Kent produces a quality of product which is in demand in foreign markets, but I do not wish in any way to imply that this is not true in other parts of Canada as well. Second, I want to illustrate that markets do exist for quality

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in saying a few words on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I would be remiss if I did not add my congratulations to you on your re-election as Speaker of the House of Commons. We all know your eminent qualifications for this position and I assure you, sir, that I am quite sincere in my remarks on this occasion. Owing to the exact similarity of our initials, sir, D.R.M., and even the similarity of Michener and Mitchell, when we were first elected to the house in 1953 we did have some difficulty in receiving each other's mail. However, I

The Address-Mr. Mitchell hasten to say that no confidences were revealed when by mistake we opened each other's correspondence. I also extend my good wishes to the Deputy Speaker and wish him well in the performance of his duties.
The purpose of my remarks this morning is to bring to the attention of hon. members the plight of the small businessman. To the best of my knowledge this point has not been touched on in the debate, possibly for the simple reason that there are not enough small businessmen in this house who would be concerned with this condition.
I think you will agree, sir, that a large proportion of the membership of the house consists of representatives of the legal profession, and for that reason I wish to draw to the attention of the house the condition of the small businessman, that being the category in which I put myself. I feel that I am speaking for many others when I refer to this situation.
In the speech from the throne mention was made of a committee to be set up to study the conditions met every day by small businessmen, with a view to improving their position. The reference in the speech from the throne is in these words:
In order to assist small business, there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. The functions of this organization will be to provide liaison between the government and small businesses, to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them.
For many years the owner of a small business has been gradually forced to the wall and has seen his business gradually shrink from a level that could be considered sufficient to supply him with a comfortable living. Many of us realize the important position of the small merchant in any community from the point of view of his fellow citizens, and although they may not be directly concerned they can see that he is gradually being forced to discontinue his retail establishment.
This is particularly true with regard to grocers who, as we know, are rapidly being forced out of business by the large chains operating in almost every one of our communities. The grocer does not have the privilege of buying in larger quantities, thereby being able to sell at a price at which he can compete with the chains, and as a non-competitor he is forced to give up his business. The same thing applies in other lines of retail merchandising which I need not mention, as I think hon. members are well acquainted with them.
At the present time, when there is considerable concern regarding a return to so-called orderly merchandising, the purpose

of this committee, after they have studied all the facts, should be to attempt to assist the small man to stay in business and thus continue to be an important cog in everyday life wherever he may have his residence. As a war measure r.p.m.-I do not mean "revolutions per minute" though in some cases I think a little more speed would be helpful-or retail price maintenance was established. It served well during the war years in assisting orderly marketing and helping provide a reasonable profit for all. It served its purpose for the time it was intended, but following the war retail price maintenance was repealed and the scheme of manufacturing, wholesaling and retailing at established prices was discontinued.
At that time it was made clear that such things as loss leaders would not be countenanced and that if such practices were prevalent and could be proved they would not be allowed to continue. However, such does not seem to be the case at the present time. Many small merchants are finding that various items on their shelves are being sold by the larger chain stores at prices with which they cannot compete. If the small merchant should attempt to sell at those prices it would mean a loss to him. I feel it is not the intention of any government to allow this situation to continue, but due to the greater buying powers of the larger organizations this condition is flourishing at the present time.
From my own experience I would mention an article that has been kicked around a great deal so far as price cutting is concerned. I refer to cigarettes. For pratically all smaller businesses the price from the wholesaler is $2.91 a carton which, if he sells individual packages, will gross him $3.30. This in itself is a very small margin, but when he runs into cut prices the situation is considerably worse. By no manipulation can I buy a carton of cigarettes for less than $2.91 but the larger outlets, being on the manufacturer's direct list, can buy them at a 10 per cent discount from the price I am forced to pay. I believe this would mean a net price of approximately $2.62 and they are being sold from $2.69 up, which still represents a profit to them but a definite loss to the small merchant.
Various other articles are in the same category of loss leaders. Possibly they could be looked upon as come-ons to get people into these places of business so they will pick up other items on which a profit can be made. If loss leader selling is to be allowed to continue I believe the combines investigation branch could take some action as I

consider that the practice, so far as the small businessman is concerned, definitely constitutes restraint of trade.
I believe that if we are to make any headway in orderly merchandising we should consider the plight of almost all merchants, other than cash businesses, arising from the fact that people are being invited to buy many articles on time payment plans with, in many cases, not even any down payment. I know that many merchants are concerned about this practice but are forced into it by their competitors. They do not like the idea, but in order to meet competition they are forced to follow suit. I also feel it has a bad moral effect on the purchasing public, in that they mortgage their incomes for some time to come to keep up the payments and therefore have no free money to spend which would assist in relieving the unemployment problem. I believe that price controls could be re-established in a great many cases. In particular, as far as a great majority of merchants are concerned, to enforce larger down payments for articles purchased on instalments would be a step in the right direction.
I must confess that I am thoroughly in accord with one of the items in the Liberal platform of the last election. I refer to the item whereby the smaller businessman when computing his income tax would be allowed accelerated depreciation on improvements, alterations, renovations and so on. This would also help to relieve the present unemployment situation by putting more local people to work, because many merchants would feel freer to undertake improvement of their merchandising facilities if relief were allowed them in the form of increased depreciation.
In comparing the plight of the small businessman in trying to compete with the large chains I must also mention the pride that the small businessman takes in his community and the help he is in all community welfare projects. You will find that he is the backbone of all local welfare campaigns, and not only gives freely of his means to various welfare endeavours but also willingly donates his services to assist in the collection of these necessary funds. In many cases he is the local chairman of such groups and assists in any way he can for the betterment of his community. Many of us can recall, when we were asked to solicit funds for say the Red Feather organization or others, that if we called on chain organizations the routine answer we would get was that the head office looked after such details. How much help to the community are these large chains? They have no local pride. Their profits go out of town, and the only benefit they produce is through the local labour they employ.
The Address-Mr. McQuillan Therefore I say that the committee the government has promised to appoint should be formed at once and study the plight of the small merchant.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must again thank the electors of my riding for re-electing me as their representative for another term in parliament. I have appreciated being their representative since 1953, and there is no other constituency I would rather represent. As you know, the Sudbury riding plays a very important part in the economic development of Canada, and with its vast resources of nickel and copper makes a very important contribution to the welfare of all Canadians. The mining industry is, of course, our largest employer of labour, with approximately
20,000	employees in this industry alone. I must say that our city continues to flourish even under the slight recession being felt in many parts of Canada. Personally I hope this is only temporary, and that all parts of Canada will return to the good times we enjoyed for many years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first to add my congratulations to the many that have already been extended to you on your election to your high office. I wish also to congratulate the Deputy Speaker and chairman of the committee of the whole. I should like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. La-freniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I am grateful for the privilege of representing Comox-Alberni in this house, and grateful as well for the opportunity of meeting other members from all over Canada. I was born in the west and spent most of my life there. I was always told that the east was completely ignorant of the problems of the west. I was told that once you got out of the Rocky mountains no one knew anything about the problems of British Columbia. During the last few years I have wondered if we were not a little ignorant, too. After having spent three weeks in Ottawa I am convinced that we are quite as ignorant of the problems of the east as the east is of the problems of the west.
I want to thank the Liberals particularly in my riding for the assistance they gave me in getting elected. I should like also to extend my condolences to the C.C.F. group upon the loss from their ranks of a man who was a very worthy opponent. He bested me in the election of 1957, but I bested him in this last election. I refer, of course, to Mr. Tom Barnett, the former member for Comox-Alberni.
618	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. McQuillan
Comox-Alberni is one of Canada's two far western constituencies. It joins the constituency of Skeena just south of the paper mill town of Ocean Falls. These two constituencies encompass the greater part of Canada's Pacific coast line. In Comox-Alberni there are something over 7,000 miles of coast. The major portion of Canada's Pacific coast fish catch is made in these waters. We in Comox-Alberni are keenly aware of the inherent problems of the fishing industry, problems that must be solved and solved soon if we are to keep this industry in its proper place in our economy.
Comox-Alberni is primarily a rugged, lumber-producing constituency. There is a small section of agricultural land along the lower east coast of Vancouver island, but generally speaking the terrain is rather rugged. There is more rock, in this area I venture to say, than in any other riding in Canada. The mountains rise from the sea to a height of many thousands of feet within a few miles of the coast, the highest being Mount Waddington at 13,249 feet. It is the highest mountain in British Columbia. These mountains are cut by a myriad of small streams and rivers, in the narrow valleys of which and extending up the mountainside to an elevation of approximately 3,000 feet grows the finest mature stand of timber in the whole of Canada.
Some of the trees are of tremendous size. I recall logging a spruce tree on the Queen Charlotte islands that had over 45,000 feet board measure of merchantable timber in it. I recall another instance of logging a huge cedar windfall on the west coast of Vancouver island, and I think there was something like 14,000 board feet in the log. There were several trees growing over this windfall, and from a ring count made on one of them it was established that the cedar tree had been on the ground for something over 800 years. From a ring count of the windfall it was established that it had been about 1,200 years old before it fell down. We removed the log and from it manufactured bevelled cedar siding. I am sure that the walls of some of the better homes in Ontario are graced with siding from that tree which started to grow over 2,000 years ago.
The logging of these huge timbers in this very rugged terrain presents a difficult problem. We have tremendous breakage and waste at which the average layman looks with horror. However, economic conditions will continue, as in the past, to govern the utilization of this timber. In recent years, as the result of mechanical advances, advances in forest chemistry and a rapidly
[Mr. McQuillan.)

increasing population on this continent, our utilization practices have improved considerably. We have far to go yet, however, before reaching a satisfactory level. I hope economic conditions will be such that we may achieve that goal.
Approximately a billion and a half feet of timber is produced in Comox-Alberni constituency, that is about half the total timber produced in the coastal forest. The value of the end product is tremendous. It is one of the great sources of wealth in Canadaj and one of the great sources of revenue for our national treasury. Many people believe that when the mature stands are logged this wealth will be exhausted. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the house that this is not true. Succeeding crops will produce far greater wealth for us than the virgin crop. Generally speaking, artificial reforestation is not required in the area. The annual increment in our own forests is undoubtedly the greatest of any forested area in the whole of Canada. When I said that artificial planting is generally not required, I should have made this reservation; except where forest fires had seriously denuded the seed crop.
At this time I should like to ask this government to give every consideration to the problem of forest protection in British Columbia, as well as all other provinces with forested areas. A great volume of the production from the area is transported to Vancouver in flat booms towed by small tugs. Many of you who have been to the coast have probably wondered what we do with all these tugs, but they tow a tremendous volume of timber down the coast every year.
There are three large pulp and paper mills in the constituency, one at Port Alice, at the extreme north end of the island, one at Campbell River, and one at Port Alberni. These mills have been greatly modernized and expanded in the last two years by a tremendous expenditure of private capital. Port Alberni has three large sawmills, a large plywood mill and a large shingle mill. It is today one of the important lumber exporting ports of the world, and as such is entitled to full consideration of its port needs by the responsible department.
The northern end of the island is undeveloped in the sense that there is a lack of roads. Most communities are isolated and can only be reached by water transport or by the use of small float planes. Consequently there is not much in the way of settled communities in the area. The labour that is used in the camps is generally of a transient nature and when the work in the camp is completed returns home to Vancouver and the lower mainland.

There is a desperate need for a road in this area. I think it would be one of the most worth-while investments that could be made by this government and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources if they were to assist the provincial government to develop this road. I am sure they would have their investment returned in very short order, as there is tremendous undeveloped wealth in the area in the form of timber and minerals. In addition, as I said before, the great part of our fish catch is made in the waters off that coast line.
At the present time there is probably a population of 7,000 people in scattered communities. I do not think there is a permanent population of that number. However, if we had proper road communications connecting the various logging camps and communities I think I am safe in saying that permanent communities would soon be established in which would dwell a population of up to
30,000	in five years; and I think I can safely say that in ten years the population would be 60,000. I believe this is exactly the kind of program the Prime Minister had in mind when proposing his national resources development program. I think this is one area that really is worthy of any expenditure made on it.
I want to ask the Minister of Transport to be ever mindful of the water and air transportation needs of the coastal area. I will agree that it has a small population and that transportation services quite often require subsidies; but when one considers the wealth that is produced per capita in that area one can see that it is worthy of investment on the part of the Department of Transport.
The forest industries of British Columbia, of which I am speaking primarily because I am familiar with them, do not ask the government to sell their product. However, they ask the government not to put any obstacles their way in selling it. They are concerned, and rightly so, about the danger of retaliatory tariffs or new tariffs for the protection of penny industries which could destroy our big dollar industries.
I have spoken previously many times, not only on political platforms but at industrial conventions, about the much talked about trade with red China. In the last couple of years Russia has begun the construction of five new pulp and paper mills on or near the borders of red China. These mills are being developed solely for the purpose of capturing the red China market. While the previous administration sat on its hands Russia got in there, recognized the potential and built these plants.
57071-3-40J
The Address-Mr. McQuillan
I am not so sure that the present administration is not sitting on its hands with regard to trade with red China. I do not advocate recognition of red China. I am not expert enough in the field of foreign affairs to be as presumptuous as that. However, I feel there is a great possibility of our developing a much larger market in red China. It has been said that if we could only get one toothpick a day into the 600 million mouths of the red Chinese the lumber industry of British Columbia would indeed be prosperous.
I want to remind the Minister of National Revenue that the forest industry is the most highly taxed industry in Canada. In British Columbia, and I believe the same situation exists in Ontario, not only is the industry subjected to the dominion or national corporate tax, but in addition we have a 10 per cent provincial corporate tax on profits from the forest industry. We also have it on the mining industry, but unfortunately in the last year or two the profits of the mining industry have been such that it has not had to pay much. I would ask him not to milk this industry dry, as it brings in more dollars through its exports than any other industry in Canada. It gives us the money with which to buy the much-needed imports that we obtain from so many other countries in the world.
At this time I should like to commend the Minister of Public Works for his housing program. A few days ago I heard one of my party colleagues rather taking the minister and his department apart with regard to their housing program, making comparisons between Canada's housing program and the United States housing program. If I remember rightly the Minister of Public Works stated that Canada expected 147,000 housing starts to be made this year. I follow quite closely the housing industry in the United States. The latest figure available to me indicates 960,000 starts in the United States. If the United States were matching Canada's program they would this year be building
1,470,000	houses. I should truly love to see this situation come about, because very shortly thereafter every whistle punk in British Columbia would have two Cadillacs in his garage.
I also want to commend the Minister of Public Works and his department for the successful removal of Ripple rock.

I have at this moment one request that I should like to make of the C.C.F. group. I believe one of the hon. members of that group is a former member of the international woodworkers of America grievance committee, and having in the past had a great deal to do with that grievance committee and knowing the kind of food they insist be put on the tables of our logging camps, I ask him as a personal favour to endeavour to get on the restaurant committee. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence I would like to nibble on this very well-gnawed procedural bone for a few minutes. I might say, in order to save the time of the house, that I sincerely endorse all congratulations and compliments which have been uttered with
[Mr. McQuillan.1
respect to the election of you, Mr. Speaker, and your deputy, and also with respect to the performance of the mover (Mr. Lafre-niere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I might explain before proceeding further that with respect to the amendment moved by the Liberal opposition, which we supported yesterday, we did support it as being a step in the right direction as we believed it would bring about some improvement in our present economic conditions. However, so far as this group are concerned we consider that amendment was like moving a motion to wash your face without any soap.
Before continuing I would like to compliment the hon. member for Comox-Alberni upon urging the government to give consideration to the expansion of trade with red China. This has been a very live issue in British Columbia, and when the hon. member urged the government to do something in this respect he was expressing the views of the great majority of the people of that province, regardless of party. I might bring to the attention of this house that the expansion of trade with red China was advocated by this group, years ago and we are delighted to know that Conservative members from the province of British Columbia are supporting us in our long-time interest in this subject. I do hope the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will be listened to with great attention, and that his suggestions will be acted upon by his colleagues on the government benches.
There has been considerable discussion with respect to the contents of the throne speech, and I am not going to be repetitious in dealing with them. Suffice it to say that we are very pleased to note there is going to be a commonwealth conference, because we in the C.C.F. are all for doing everything we can to expand trade within the commonwealth. We are also glad to note there is provision for the introduction of a measure concerning a bill of rights. This is a bit of an enigma at present, for while we like the principle being endorsed in so far as it is announced in the throne speech, we will have to await the details to see if we are satisfied that it will be the kind of bill of rights which we think should be introduced.
We were very glad to note the amendment suggested to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. Such an amendment has been suggested by members of this group for many years, and once again we are glad that even with our small numbers we have had some influence on the former Liberal government and on the present overwhelming Conservative

majority. We are glad to see amendments proposed to the veterans legislation, and I am sure that members in all parts of the house will welcome some improvement in this legislation. We trust the amendments will be in accord with the recommendations of the Canadian Legion and the national council of veterans.
Then there is also provision for an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and I am sure my colleagues from the prairie provinces are looking forward to a full discussion of this question, because if there is one thing that is certain it is that none of our colleagues from the prairie provinces can ever be accused of under-debating any question coming before this house which concerns the prairie farmers and their problems.
We are also very pleased to see that at last provision is to be made for a standing committee on veterans affairs. This measure was advocated by the members of the present government party and the C.C.F. and others in this house for years, when we stood together in opposition, and I and my colleagues are very gratified that we are at least going to have such a standing committee to review annually the problems of the veterans, taking into account the conditions and circumstances which change from time to time.
We are particularly interested in the suggestion in the throne speech that the government intends to further a program of government investment through crown corporations, direct government activity and activity in co-operation with provincial governments. I might say this development is of great interest to many of my constituents, and I wish to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the government a number of projects which could be undertaken in the very near future as part of this national investment program. In doing so I want to remind the government that they can well afford to undertake some very heavy expenditures in Kootenay West, which is one of the great wealth-producing areas of Canada. I think it is correct to say that in this constituency the residents pay the largest per capita income tax of any constituency in Canada.
First of all, and because of my own great interest in British Columbia and particularly in my constituency, I would like to mention the development of the water resources of the Columbia river, and in that connection we all primarily think of the building, we trust very soon, of the Mica creek dam. This has been under discussion for years; the international joint commission has been conducting surveys since 1945 in co-operation with other government departments, and the
The Address-Mr. Herridge information is all now available. All that requires to be done is the drafting of the plans and so on, as soon as the governments of Canada and the United States come to a mutually satisfactory agreement respecting adequate payment for the downstream benefits in the United States. We do urge the government to make haste in this respect, and we look forward to an announcement very soon by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources as indicated in his reply to a question I asked of him some two weeks ago.
In addition, we have a very important airport at Castlegar which requires some urgent improvements. The lengthening of the runway is an urgent necessity in order to meet the needs of the larger planes landing there; and radio truck guidance, I am informed, is urgently required because of the position of the airport between two ranges of mountains and the fact that there is very little opportunity to manoeuvre in the space between these mountains. I am also informed that the expansion and black-topping of the runways is necessary, and I put this forward as another project which might be undertaken in the very near future as part of this national investment program.
I am also glad to suggest again the extension of the application of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to all provinces in Canada. This is of very vital concern to many of the people I represent since we have some wonderful lands which are underdeveloped because the act has not been applicable to all provinces. We hear of great expansions in the north with railways running almost to the unknown and great expenditures in isolated places. While we are most anxious to see such improvements and the development of the northern part of our country progressing, we want to bring to the attention of the government the fact that even in constituencies such as Kootenay West there are thousands of acres of land close to transportation which could be developed at relatively little cost, but which are at present lying idle.
I would like to bring forward one or two illustrations. First of all I will deal with the Slocan valley, which is a beautiful valley in my constituency about 30 miles long and varying from one to one and a half miles wide. The whole floor of that beautiful valley is covered with good soil. The Slocan river flows through the centre. The whole valley is served with power, and in addition there is a paved highway and a railroad running the whole length of the valley. Yet with all those facilities provided at public expense, under present conditions a great portion of the acreage in the valley is lying

The Address-Mr. Herridge idle, in fallow, because of the necessity for certain flood control, some minor diking and some drainage operations. I suggest to the government that we need an extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to meet situations like this, where the expenditure of a relatively small amount of money will bring into production thousands of acres of fertile land which is at present lying idle.
I wish now to deal with the Lardeau valley, another beautiful valley in my constituency. In fact perhaps I should remind new hon. members that I represent Canada's garden of Eden. This valley is also about 30 miles long and contains approximately 16,000 acres of first-class agricultural land, a fact which I have had carefully checked, of which approximately 15,000 are completely unused at the present time. A river and a gravel road run the entire length of the valley, and there is an excellent school. The total permanent population is about 150 persons. Here are thousands of acres of good land close to transportation simply awaiting the expenditure of a relatively small amount of money to bring that extremely fertile soil into production. What is necessary there is the deepening of the bed of the Duncan river, and some drainage and diking for flood control purposes.
To illustrate how little money is required to provide almost exceptional results, I would point out that during the last four or five years the Department of Public Works has been straightening the course of the Duncan river and lowering its bed in a few places in order to provide for the passage of booms, small boats and transportation of that kind. This was done at a cost of approximately $5,000 a year and primarily for the purpose of providing access from Kootenay lake to Howser lake, but the secondary result of that small expenditure was to lower the water table around Meadow Creek, which is about the centre of the valley, by about three feet so that thousands of acres of land can now be cultivated to much greater advantage than they could previously. I do hope the government will give consideration to the opportunities that exist for public investment to public advantage in the Lardeau valley.
Turning now to the subject of provincial parks, we have some beautiful ones in the Kootenays which at the present time are largely unknown to a great majority of the people who live in the district, and certainly to most tourists who visit our area, because of the lack of access roads. I refer in the first instance to the Kokanee park near Nelson, a park of magnificent glaciers and mountain scenery and all those things which delight the eyes of those who relish mountain climbing and recreation of that sort. All that

is required to make that park available for the enjoyment of large numbers of Canadians is the building of a satisfactory access road. In view of the present government's indicated willingness to co-operate with provincial governments in the building of access roads to parks I urge the government to give consideration to co-operating with the provincial government in the building of an access road to Kokanee park.
Another beautiful park is Nakusp hot springs provincial park. I happen to have been the chairman of the board of commissioners of this park from 1925 until three years ago. This lovely park has several hot springs within its confines the chemical content of which I am told is about of equal value to those of Radium. It is in a delightful location, and you can sit by the side of the Kuskanox river that flows for 30 miles and is stocked with brook trout, actually catch a trout in the stream and simply swing it over and cook it in the hot springs. Where else in Canada could you find similar opportunity. I ask the federal government to give consideration to co-operation with the provincial government in the building of an access road to Nakusp hot springs provincial park, another of these beauty spots almost unknown to the majority of Canadians.
There are great opportunities for public investment in roads. I know that federal government policy to date has been to confine its efforts with respect to the building of roads largely to co-operation with the provinces in the building of the trans-Canada highway, and to roads required in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. However, we in this group think that because of the great need for roads in this country and the fact that the building of many of these roads is obviously beyond the capacity of provincial governments the policy should be changed to include the building of north-south roads connecting with the trans-Canada highway and the other trans-Canada highways which we trust will be built in the near future.
In this connection I want to bring to the attention of the house the Inonoaklin valley, which is about 15 miles long and 1J miles wide, containing thousands of acres of first-class land much of which is being farmed at the present time. Here again, however, these very diligent and hard-working pioneer farmers are denied the opportunity to succeed because of the lack of access to markets for their dairy and poultry products, beef and other agricultural commodities. These markets, of course, are to the south in the industrial areas of Trail and Nelson, but because there is no road many farmers are finding it difficult to make a bare living. There is an opportunity for the building of a road

here which would be part of the north-south road connecting with the trans-Canada highway at Revelstoke, and which would provide access to satisfactory markets for a good number of the farmers in that area.
To illustrate the situation, I might mention that there is a great deal of hay produced in that area. Last winter and at the present time there are hundreds of tons of surplus hay in the farmers' barns in that district. That is hay over and above that required to feed the stock in the valley. There is a good market for hay within 90 miles. The reason the hay remains in the farmers' barns is that the cost of transporting it is so great that it does not pay to ship the hay to the market. It has to be transported by boat a distance of about 40 miles. The cost of shipping it by boat that short distance exceeds the cost of transporting it hundreds of miles on the Canadian Pacific Railway. The construction of an access road about 25 miles in length would connect that valley with the markets that are required for the prosperity and well-being of those farmers. I urge the government to consider extending assistance to provincial governments for the building of such roads.
There is one other matter of importance with which I wish to deal. I am presenting these matters to the government of the day as opportunities which I trust it will seize with both hands. About 5,000 of my constituents have been denied satisfactory radio reception ever since radio reception became possible in Canada. Because of the strength of radio signals from United States stations many of my constituents in the northern portion of the Kootenays are denied the opportunity of listening to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation after dark, and during the day the reception is far from satisfactory. In view of the report of the royal commission on television and broadcasting, and in view of the minister's reply to my repeated questions in the house, I do urge that the government consider the early provision of satisfactory radio reception to the 5,000 of my constituents denied that opportunity at the present time, as part of a public investment program in Canada.
With these very limited requests, Mr. Speaker-I think they are most modest-I now want to turn in another direction. I might say that I am sorry I was not in the house yesterday when the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), spoke. I must say that I know he has the respect of all hon. members, and as far as this group is concerned, their affection. Two of us-my seatmate, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and
The Address-Mr. Herridge myself-came to the house as freshmen members when the hon. gentleman first arrived. Naturally we know one another very well.
I was particularly disappointed at not being present in the house when he spoke yesterday but, as usual, I had a valid excuse. I had some very interesting and important people from the city of Toronto, connected with a strictly non-political organization, come to see me about a matter of serious concern to many Canadians. I had to listen to their representations, and they were very pleased to listen to my advice and suggestions. However, owing to that unexpected interruption at an unfortunate time, so far as my opportunity to listen to the hon. member for Greenwood was concerned, I missed what I found on reading Hansard this morning were his most enjoyable remarks.
I noticed, Mr. Speaker, that he made some reference to the members of the C.C.F. group in a very kindly way, as he usually does. He told a story, something to the effect-we also had very similar war experiences-that owing to battle casualties, on one occasion the rum rations came up for a full company when there were only seven or eight left after the battle had ended. He said the seven or eight consumed the rations sent up to the line for a full company, and as a consequence momentarily lost all their terror and fears of war, and so on. The hon. member rather indicated that that simile could be applied to the C.C.F. because we are few in number. He suggested that we were given rations of information from a rearguard outside this building, which removed our fear of the overwhelming majority of the Conservative party.
I want to tell him that I had a similar experience to his during the battle of the Somme. Our company was very severely decimated during one attack, and a very few men in the company had the rum rations which were originally intended for the almost full strength of the company before it went into action. In this case the rum rations came into the hands of a well-known sergeant whom the Minister of Public Works knew quite well. He tried to drink the full rum jar himself. He did not believe in the redistribution of wealth; and I can well understand it, Mr. Speaker, because at the very time he was serving in the forces he was the president of the local Conservative association in his district.
I have listened with great interest to this debate, Mr. Speaker, and to the contribution made by the new members. I well understand their fear when making a speech in the House of Commons for the first time; but I must say that some of them, in their references to this group, exposed their ignorance and indicated

The Address-Mr. Herridge that they misunderstood what the C.C.F. stand for and what this group advocates and stands for in the House of Commons. I presume that would be occasioned by the environment of Conservative campaign headquarters, which would not be a very suitable atmosphere for the development of logical thinking and thought.

I am very sorry; I always like to be heard and I want to be heard. Perhaps the policies of this movement, shall I say, in total were first brought to the attention of this house, or introduced in this house, on March 2, 1932, as the result of a debate on a motion moved by the late J. S. Woods-worth; and for the information of the neophytes in the house I am going to read it. It will be found at page 726 of Hansard of 1932. Mr. Woodsworth moved as follows:
Whereas under our present economic arrangement large numbers of our people are unemployed and without the means of earning a livelihood for themselves and their dependants;
And whereas the prevalence of the present depression throughout the world indicates fundamental defects in the existing economic system;
Be it therefore resolved: That, in the opinion of this house the government should immediately take measures looking to the setting up of a co-operative commonwealth in which all natural resources and the socially necessary machinery of production will be used in the interests of the people and not for the benefit of the few.
I say to hon. gentlemen that he was not suggesting that all property and real estate should be publicly owned, but that all property be used in the interests of the people. Undoubtedly the capitalist system has a great many achievements to its credit. I suppose it is correct to say that the problem of production has been largely solved, but the problem of distribution at home and abroad is still unsolved and that is why members of this group advocate the economic policies they do. To prove that point I want to quote from a speech made by a former prominent Progressive Conservative cabinet minister. Mr. H. H. Stevens, former minister of trade and commerce, in a speech to the Empire club in Toronto on October 8, 1930, had this to say:
While one-third of the human race, which might be termed western civilization, including Europe and North America, has so perfected the system of mechanized production that it has more goods than it can consume or sell, the other two-thirds of the human race, which can be classified as eastern civilization, is in dire need of those things which lie rotting in the possession of the other division, and over the whole human race hangs, like a funeral pall, want, poverty, idleness and social disintegration.
That is exactly what is occurring in many sections of the east at present. There has

been very little improvement in the capitalist system and the conditions complained of in this speech by a former minister of trade and commerce in a Conservative administration.
I want to give one other quotation before coming to my brief remarks. Professor Blackett, who is very well known, recently said according to the Economist of September 7, 1957:
The uneven division of power and wealth, the wide differences of power and comfort among the nations of mankind, are the sources of discord in the modern world, its major challenge and, unrelieved, its moral doom.
This is the condition we in this group aim to correct, and it is one of the serious problems that face us at the present time. You know hon. gentlemen, when they were speaking in support of the capitalist system and in criticism of the policies of this group, spoke as if the capitalist system was devised when Adam and Eve were on the earth. As a matter of fact capitalism is a relatively new institution in the history of the human race.
I suppose there were many centuries of feudalism, but I think it is safe to say that capitalism began about 1769, with the advent of the steam engine. So we have had about 189 years of a capitalist society, a very short time in the total lifetime of the human race.
What do we in this group aim to do? I want to deal with that very briefly and then go on to another topic in which we are particularly interested. I am giving this more in the nature of a lecture to a class in economics. We in the C.C.F. aim to develop a politically moral society as distinct from the present politically unctuous society. I think the word "unctuous" is a good word when you listen to some of the statements made by members on the government side with such self-satisfaction, with almost an air of superiority and such confidence in the belief that the Progressive Conservative party is going to be in power from now until eternity.
I must say that we respect the honest convictions of all persons who aim to use our constitutional and parliamentary procedures to improve our social order. We do not question the purpose, intention or integrity of the hon. gentlemen opposite us. We question their judgment, their knowledge of economic history and their understanding of economic and social development today. What does the C.C.F. aim to do?

The C.C.F. offers its program as an alternative to the political dictatorship

of communism and the economic dictatorship of monopoly capitalism. While we hear repeatedly of the free enterprise society and that the hon. gentlemen support the free enterprise society, if you study the facts you know that the genuine free enterprise sections of our economy are being erased, shall I say, day after day by the increasing economic power of fewer and fewer corporations in every industry in North America.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is fair to say that our program is based on an understanding of Canadian history, Canadian traditions and Canadian psychology. We offer it as a democratic socialist alternative to the policies advanced by the two major parties. There is some difference between our party and the other parties. Our policies are devised at biennial conventions on the national level and at annual conventions on the provincial level. Our policies are the result of long and full discussion at these conventions.
We are often criticized for not being democratic. Well, the convention, the opportunity to discuss and decide, is considered the basis of a democratic society. What about the Liberal party? 1 think it has had four national conventions when it wanted to elect new leaders since 1896. What about the Conservative party? They must be given credit for having had one or two more conventions, but only because they change their leaders more frequently. Anyway, that is the basis of our program and our policy in the federal and provincial fields.
What about financial support? The major parties willingly admit how they obtain their contributions. A prominent member of the Progressive Conservative organization in my constituency informed me of the large contributions received from a certain company in British Columbia, and he considered it was quite proper and quite fair. Where do we get our contributions? We get our contributions from the members and supporters of the C.C.F. or in some cases from people who partly believe in our program but think we are going in the right direction and so on. Ours is a collection of small amounts from the people. Therefore we respond naturally to those people who have indicated their support in that way, as possibly others will respond to the sources from which their campaign funds come.
What do we propose? We propose a mixed economy as the best approach to economic and social problems at the present time, an economy which will contain an expanding area of public ownership in the federal, provincial and municipal fields wherever private interests fail to accept their responsibilities, or wherever it is clearly indicated that it is in the public interest and to the
The Address-Mr. Herridge public advantage to develop a certain project or industry under public ownership. We believe in a great expansion of co-operative ownership because we believe that co-operative ownership is a training ground in the administration of public affairs.

Mr. Speaker, when the house recessed at one o'clock for bodily sustenance I was just dealing with the triple aspects of the C.C.F. domestic program which we term the mixed economy. 1 had dealt briefly with the matter of public ownership and was then dealing with the question of co-operative ownership, in which the C.C.F. is very seriously concerned. I was going to say that the C.C.F. believes in a vast expansion of co-operative ownership and development in Canada, not as the result of a reluctant government passing legislation that makes this type of ownership legal, but as the result of education, sponsorship and financial assistance on the part of the respective governments concerned.
In addition to the economic values of cooperative ownership to the people of Canada, we believe there is a great value in its development of the understanding of democratic processes, because in co-operative ownership people have an opportunity to understand the administration of democratic procedures both on the political and administrative levels.
Third, we in the C.C.F. believe there is a tremendous opportunity for the expansion of what we term legitimate private or free enterprise. What we mean by that is a situation in which there is a genuine element of competition; where there is no exploitation of the community as the result of monopoly, and where there is a service rendered to the community as there is at present by many small businessmen operating industries, services and things of that sort. Where there is a genuine expression of the principle of competition we believe there is a great opportunity for the expansion of legitimate free enterprise.
As my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker, I must conclude my explanation of C.C.F. policy. I see a member applauding the fact that my time is drawing to a close, and I am rather disappointed. I suggest to the new members of the Progressive Conservative party-I have given up suggesting it to the ancient members of the Liberal party- that if they want to understand our program

Moving from the general to the particular, in view of our great interest in things that are of immediate concern and interest to the Canadian people from day to day, I want to deal briefly with a problem which is of increasing concern to the municipalities across Canada. That is the shortage of funds with which to carry on properly the functions for which they were created. I am reminded of this subject particularly in view of a recent report by the Bank of Canada which I read in yesterday's Gazette. It reads:
Canada's municipalities are going deeper into debt. The money they owed for schools, roads and other essentials rose to $3,128,300,000 at the end of 1957 from $2,785,200,000 at the end of 1956, the Bank of Canada reported today.
I have not the time to elaborate or explain the difficulties facing municipalities. All hon. members know them. We in the C.C.F. believe in action in this respect because of the urgency of this situation. I listened with interest this morning to the Prime Minister suggesting he was going to call an informal conference in September. As a matter of fact, it reminded me of a meeting called in the parish hall by the district nurse for mothers with undernourished children in order to discuss a new bottle formula they will have the opportunity of purchasing at the corner drug store.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue):
That the following words be added to the address:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the advisability of presenting legislation at this session to relieve the very heavy financial burden now carried by the municipalities of this country.

Mr. Speaker, may I associate myself with all those hon. members who paid their respects to you on the occasion of your unanimous re-election to the high office of Speaker of the House of Commons. Even my brief and cursory exposure to this house has been sufficient to convince me how well-founded is your reputation for learning, urbanity and fairness.
I take pleasure also in extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne upon the distinguished manner in which they carried out their tasks. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency displayed a wit and eloquence which we expect of members from la belle province. The hon. member for Yukon has the unenviable reputation of having fought


three elections in the space of nine months, and proved himself to be a formidable speaker, a worthy representative of that rugged land.
To the people of Stormont I extend sincere thanks for their support and the assurance that they can count on me at all times to do whatever can be done to help my county and my country. The constituency which I have the honour to represent and serve comprises the whole of the county of Stormont which, along with Glengarry on the east and Dundas on the west, makes up the historic "old eastern district." This area so aptly described as the cradle of Ontario, is equally the cradle of the western provinces. The epitome of this fact is the little village of St. Andrews, about 70 miles southwest of here at the southern end of the county, where both John Sandfield Macdonald, the first premier of Ontario, and Simon Fraser, the celebrated explorer, lie buried. Most of the Nor-West partners either originated in or retired to this area. I could mention many, but the names of William MacGillivray, Angus McGillis, David Thomson, MacDonald of Garth and John Duncan Campbell will suffice. Incidentally, sir, the latter was my greatgrandfather and MacDonald was his father in law.
The earliest pioneers in many parts of the prairies were transplanted from this area, as were the first gold miners in the Kootenays and the Cariboo, such as Cariboo Cameron. The original settlers in Stormont, amongst them my ancestors on both sides of the family, were Highlanders and Palatinates who were forced by the American revolution to abandon their homes in the Mohawk valley for the wilderness of Upper Canada. These hardy Scotch and Dutoh people, along with their French Canadian compatriots who now make up 53.9 per cent of the population of my home town of Cornwall, share the unique distinction of being the only people in the civilized world who have never lived under a republican form of government. The English, after a disastrous experience with Cromwell, have not repeated their mistake.
On July 1 of this year the land on which many of these Stormont pioneers and their descendants have lived will disappear forever beneath the waters of the St. Lawrence as 34,000 acres of land on both sides of the border are inundated within four days. At 4 a.m. on this date a button will be pushed on the Iroquois control dam lifting massive steel gates to let a flow of water from lake Ontario enter the huge lake which will be formed as a reservoir for the power plant at Cornwall. The most dramatic moment in the whole four-year job of building the

St. Lawrence seaway and power project is scheduled for 8 a.m., when 30 tons of explosives will blast two 100-foot gaps in the earthen cofferdam that blocks off the powerhouse area.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the city council and the good people of Cornwall may I extend a very warm invitation to as many hon. members as can escape from their onerous duties to attend the inundation ceremonies this July 1 to 4. Our Prime Minister, the lieutenant governor and premier of Ontario and many other dignitaries have graciously consented to attend. I can assure you that both bread and circuses will be provided for your enjoyment and that there will be everything from street dancing to- well, you name it.
Despite some misunderstanding and even injustices inevitable in an undertaking of this size, the Ontario hydro has dealt generously with the people displaced by this project, as is evidenced by the splendid modern communities of Ingleside and Long Sault in which they now live. However, I am not one of those who tend to confuse all changes with progress. We must ensure that the people of Canada, and particularly my constituents who have endured the most, derive the maximum benefit from this vast undertaking. Already some sectional United States interests, the same selfish interests which were violently opposed to the seaway itself and delayed its construction for more than two decades, are trying to promote prohibitive tolls.
The seaway project was advocated and nationally supported in Canada almost entirely on the ground of national defence and because it would increase and improve domestic transportation facilities. The new seaway will in many important instances offer no new benefits to present users. Tolls will only add unnecessarily to the cost of many raw materials which have always been carried through the existing waterways without charges on cargoes. The bulk commodities used by many industries in the lake Ontario area will suffer unfair and costly disadvantage from a toll-encumbered seaway, as will the package freight trade between all Canadian ports from Montreal to the great lakes. The suggestion of tolls was entirely a United States concept, and their acceptance would be unjust and inequitable to Canada, especially on the basis of a joint toll system. Whereas the United States will require to recover only $130 million to repay their costs, there is owing to Canada something in the neighbourhood of $300 million.
To meet these United States terms toll charges would have to be set so high that the seaway would attract little if any traffic
The Address-Mr. G. Campbell in addition to the present freight volume. The effect of this would be to penalize present Canadian users severely without providing any corresponding benefits. Toll rates as recommended by the toll committees who are studying this matter at this time will undoubtedly be proposed on the basis of expected traffic volume. Since future traffic will vary in direct ratio to the economic advantages offered by this new seaway, there will be no reliable guide for estimates based on arbitrarily established toll rates. Trade and traffic patterns take a long time to establish themselves. Once set, they are extremely difficult to change. The immediate imposition of tolls even of an ostensibly reasonable nature might conceivably nullify both the immediate and the long-term benefits that Canada has every right to expect from the seaway. If shipping shuns the seaway from the beginning because of tolls, it might take a very long time indeed to lure it back.
May I therefore respectfully suggest that the best action for our government to take at this stage may very well be to adopt the recommendations made by the toll committees but to suspend the implementation of any toll charges until a reliable traffic pattern has emerged. This procedure is entirely within Canada's rights as a principal partner in the seaway. It should apply to the Welland canal and all seaway locks under Canadian administration, regardless of what is done in the two United States operated locks.
May I also say that some of my constituents regard the huge seaway headquarters building in Cornwall as a monument erected to himself by a former illustrious minister of transport. Others regard this same building as a poor consolation prize for the loss of the canal at Cornwall to the Americans. Rightly or wrongly they attribute the amazing expansion of Massena, New York from a country crossroads to an industrial metropolis to the proximity of this canal. Meanwhile Cornwall has acquired not a single major industry since the last war, and unemployment has been chronic during most of this period.
I look forward to the time when many of these difficulties will be rectified by the construction of an all-Canadian seaway, for which provision has been made by removable gates in the diversion canal which intersects the dike at Cornwall and by the dredging of a 27 foot draft canal in the adjacent natural waters. In addition to the much needed employment which would be provided in the Cornwall area, I understand there are very substantial technical advantages to be derived from a Canadian canal. The downstream entrance would be in slack water and the

The Address-Mr. G. Campbell restricted channel would be confined to a distance of three miles, as compared to 15 miles in the United States system.
Regardless of how soon the all-Canadian seaway is built, my constituents would derive great benefit from the construction of harbour facilities east of Cornwall where shipping turns south to enter the United States canal, and where in the event of a future Canadian canal it would continue west. Such docking space would doubtless create its own traffic, and would be a tremendous inducement to new industry to locate in this area.
This harbour project, in conjunction with a new direct highway linking Ottawa with the partially constructed high level international bridge at Cornwall, which highway I hope and trust the province of Ontario has under consideration at this time, would hasten the realization of our dream of eastern Ontario as a golden triangle of thriving industries, prosperous farms and natural playgrounds. The products of the Ottawa valley would have an outlet at Cornwall both to the United States by road and to the rest of the world by water and tourists in vast number would De attracted via Cornwall or Kingston to the beauties of the Canadian capital, the Rideau inkes, the Thousand islands and the seaway park system.
It was with great satisfaction that I heard in the speech from the throne of the great public works program to be initiated by this government. I am confident that it will give serious consideration not only to these harbour facilities but to the construction of air strips and navigational aids at Cornwall. I believe that a municipal airport would put Cornwall on the air map and would help this area to achieve the glowing potential which is its destiny.
I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to be a supporter of the first government in 30 years to represent all the people of Canada, and the first government in 30 years that has representation from every province in this vast dominion stretching from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth. Two of the problems which have haunted this country since its inception have been largely solved by the victory of the Conservative party under the inspired leadership of our Prime Minister on March 31 of this year. Implicit in confederation are two assumptions; first, a working agreement on the division of powers between the federal and provincial governments, and second, a degree of tolerance as between the two main cultural groups of this country. This election has established the validity of Bamum's dictum, "You can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time,


but you can't fool all the people all the time". The old Liberal tactic of divide et impero, of playing one part of the country against the other and of exaggerating sectional and cultural cleavages, is finished. The flood waters of Conservatism have left the Liberals stranded high and dry like branches on a dead tree and have inundated the party of the left. The Progressive Conservative party has come to power and it has done so on the basis of a very general support. It cannot be said that this party won its victory because it was the representative of business or of the affluent classes in Canadian society. It could never have attained this power without the support of a very large part of the labour vote, without a large percentage of the farm vote, and without the support of that other labour class which does not like to be called labour and which suffers more for its pretensions than any other class in this country, the white collar class.
I believe one of the significant aspects of this election was something that, judging from the labour congress which has just come to an end in Winnipeg, the labour leaders have not yet assessed themselves. That is, that the labour population of this country does not follow either its elected or its intellectual leadership. I must confess that I am puzzled about this, but when one looks at the voting history of labour in Canada one must see that with few exceptions it has never supported the C.C.F., which group has often been called the political arm of labour. In Windsor in the last election people supported the Liberals, as they had for years, and in other main industrial centres such as Vancouver, Montreal, Hamilton and Toronto, they helped to pile up this huge majority for the Conservative party. Maybe it is true after all, as many people have said on this continent, that labour at the present time is one of the Conservative forces in our society. A recent Gallup poll indicates that 49 per cent of the labour vote in this country went to Conservatives, so if we have a labour party in Canada at the present time it is the Progressive Conservative party.

This, Mr. Speaker, is what labour said when it spoke with its vote and this, I am pleased to say, is one of the reasons I am standing here today.
I wish to urge an expansion of our domestic consumption, but if we are to have such expansion I believe our government must give thought to something which has not been mentioned in the speech from the throne. That is an adjustment of the profit structure existing in our economy. I consider that one of the main causes of the depression of

1929 and of our present recession is the fact that when profits become too large and, as a result, are indiscriminately salted away or ploughed back into producer industry, the consumer does not then have enough money to consume all the goods which our economy produces.
