The only way we are able to consume all the goods Canadian and United States factories produce in such vast quantities is by borrowing, and this condition has caused inflation. I believe it is apparent, if we are willing to face this fact, that a lot of the people who have washing machines and refrigerators, television sets and automobiles, have them not because they have enough money to pay for them but because they are borrowing on next year's income. As long as we maintain an economy on borrowed money we will have to borrow more and more money until the time comes when nobody will lend. When all your salary is going for what you bought two years ago you cannot buy anything now. This, in essence, is just what has happened in Canada and in the United States.
The only way we could consume the goods we are able to produce is if we were to raise the income of the average member of our society to the point where he could buy these things without borrowing. It should be understood, and perhaps it is understood, by those who are in a position to reap profits that if this capitalistic, industrial society of ours is to work then there must be an adjustment downward in those profits. Since world war II it has been very easy to see that the profits of large corporations have spiralled upward at the same rate that those receiving those profits have complained about the spiralling of inflation. Inflation is caused when people continue to buy and consume goods even when they are not earning sufficient to pay for them, and this adjustment must be made if our economy is to enjoy the benefits of full prosperity and employment.
I was most impressed by the government's plan for the development of our north country, but I have been perturbed by some of the talk accompanying this hoped-for development. Such talk is confined to the prospect of digging up minerals and selling them. We should, however, remember that digging up minerals is not going to help our present unemployment problem very much until we can sell the minerals we have already dug out of the earth. I trust any development of the north will be of a kind which will lend itself to the development of consumer industries as well as producer industries in that territory.
The Address-Mr. G. Campbell
We have reached the point where we are really facing a major decision, as to whether we shall remain a country which produces raw material or whether we shall try to develop more fully into a country which processes more of our raw material, thereby developing its own culture and civilization. In all history there is no record of a country ever becoming great by exporting its material resources in their raw state. I know there are grave problems involved in this development, but I believe they can be overcome by a government which has vision and courage.
I was very glad to note in' the speech from the throne that the most obvious and necessary consumer industry, that of home building, has received increased assistance. There has been a very tangible example of such assistance in my own constituency iri the recent announcement by the Minister of Public Works on behalf of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation arid by the Ontario minister of planning and development with respect to the construction in Cornwall of subsidized low-rental housing comprising 125 units at an estimated cost of approximately $1 million. This is in addition to a 300-unit federal-provincial project already approved in March of this year.
In my constituency the unemployment situation is critical. In Cornwall, the only town of any size-having a population of approximately 41,000 people-there are three main industries; Howard Smith Paper Mills Limited, Canadian Textiles Limited and Cour-tauld's Canada Limited. The latter two are textile firms and the three plants normally employ in the neighbourhood of 2,000 men each. The pulp and paper mill is in a relatively buoyant condition, but the condition of the two textile mills could only be described as distressing.
There are certain misconceptions about the textile industry, especially the primary cotton manufacturing industry, which must be cleared up before any realistic appraisal can be made of the situation. First it must be emphasized, as was substantiated by the Gordon commission, that Canadian textile mills are not only among the most efficiently organized in the industry, but they are also well equipped to produce the highest quality textile products. A number of mills have closed down due to foreign pressure and tight money. When these casualties are discussed they are attributed to the change in trends in consumer uses of synthetics. In fact, however, the new uses for nylon, orlon and the other synthetic fabrics, particularly when blended with the older natural fibres like wool and cotton, have actually strengthened the industry, not weakened it. The manufacturers who use synthetic fibres almost exclusively,

The Address-Mr. G. Campbell have been among the hardest hit in bearing the brunt of this foreign competition.
The producers of Europe and Asia enjoy many advantages over Canadian mills, in that they all pay much lower wages and most are subsidized in one form or another by their governments. United States producers, of course, have the economies of specialization and large scale production due to their vast markets.
Second, and contrary to the opinion of our predecessors on this side of the house, the textile industry is not expendable. In fact since world war II the Canadian industry has actually invested well over $400 million in new plants, equipment and processes. Do not let anyone tell you that the textile people are giving up after more than 100 years of operation in this country! This industry is vital to our economy for several reasons. It is uniquely Canadian in that about 80 per cent of its equity stock is owned by Canadians. It is not subject to the seasonal fluctuations that have plagued the producer industries in this country. It is centred in the smaller towns where there is no alternative source of employment. And finally, it employs a large number of female and unskilled labour which could not find employment elsewhere.
Cotton production is as native to Canada as it is to Lancashire, and dates from the same period. For that matter, it is as native to Canada as aluminum. The cotton textile industry alone comprises 76 mills mostly located in Ontario and Quebec, and it employs
23,000	people while about 88,000 are employed in the whole industry in normal times.
Prior to the war the Canadian cotton mills supplied over 70 per cent of the total cotton fabric market in this country. Today, however, their share is under 50 per cent of the over-all Canadian market. From a total value of $15,500,000 in 1939, United States textile imports into this country have risen to $145 million in 1956; from approximately $15 million to approximately $145 million within a few short years. Canada has become the third largest net importer of cotton goods in the world. Only Australia and Indonesia import more, and neither of those countries has a cotton textile industry of its own.
The third misconception about this industry is that they are urging the construction of a high tariff wall to shelter them from the winds of competition. In fact, however, the proposals made by the cotton producers to the tariff board which is presently sitting are designed to correct anomalies, to rectify unplanned and accidental developments, to take account of technological changes and generally to catch up with the last 30 years since the tariff schedule was last studied as a whole.
[Mr. Campbell (Stormont) .1
Some increases in duty rates are proposed but there are also some decreases proposed, and in some places no change is suggested. Although the cotton tariff schedule has changed little in more than 30 years the industry is stressing before the tariff board that there has been one change of great importance. This is a change in the wording of the tariff item on coloured fabrics, made in the United States trade treaty of 1939. Until that time these cloths were classified in a single tariff item without regard to their value. In 1939 the tariff was divided so that the goods of the lowest value per pound received unchanged protection but reduced duties were provided on higher priced specialty fabrics. Now, with the price increases which have taken place since, almost all imported fabrics are in the higher priced class so naturally they come under the lowest rate of duty.
This means that the reasonable protection intended in 1939 to cover most coloured fabrics made in Canada now covers practically none at all. Instead, almost all are imported at the low rates intended for a few high priced specialties. In any new tariff schedule it is probably preferable that fabrics be classified by construction rather than by value brackets, which could quickly become meaningless by reason of price changes.
Dumping, particularly from the United States, is a major concern of the cotton textile industry. The present anti-dumping regulations can be invoked only if the export sale price of the foreign made product is less than the average price for which it was sold during the previous six months in the home market of the exporter. These regulations can be circumvented in so many ways that it has thrown an almost impossible task on the customs people. Probably the most effective measure would be a return to the original anti-dumping regulations enforced before 1948, which required that the export price include the full cost of manufacturing plus a markup for distribution, selling and profit, together with an adequate customs staff to enforce them. Due to overproduction and the chaotic state of the United States textile industry there has been a flood of imports into Canada recently. The United States mills are actually exporting their depression to Canada. The need for action is urgent.
As my time has just about expired, Mr. Speaker, I shall have to consider the problems of the dairy farmers in my constituency at a later date. I might say that although the agricultural price stabilization bill was generally welcomed by farmers, many adjustments in the administration of the legislation remain to be made before the primary-producer can derive full benefits.

In closing, if what I have said does not sufficiently explain to hon. members of the opposition why they are sitting where they are, another reason is that the people of Canada were tired of being manipulated. They want to be led, and they find in the Prime Minister, as their fathers found in Sir John A. Macdonald, a man with many human weaknesses, generous in his instincts, with the courage to tell us that materialism is not enough; one possessed of that vision without which the people perish, who can express that vision in lofty words and translate it into effective action.
As hon. gentlemen opposite are so anxious to point out, our Prime Minister is probably embarassed by the great numbers and high quality of his supporters.
We must not abuse our powers as others before us have done; but we must be careful that in trying like Caesar's wife to be above reproach we do not stultify action, necessary action, even on controversial problems. Great power can also be a power for good.
The immense resources of talent, youthful vigour and idealism available to this government give it a magnificent opportunity to accomplish great things. I for one would much rather see it go down in history as a government that did many great and good things, even though it made great mistakes, than as a government which never made a mistake because it attempted nothing and achieved nothing. With great privilege comes great responsibility. This is a time for greatness, and the heirs of Macdonald and Disraeli should not shrink from it.

I refer to a throughway for Montreal. It would cover, all told, about 14 miles from east to west. It would start at the provincial highway, across Montreal West, follow the street-car tracks along the Lachine canal, then run along St. Ambroise street, Notre Dame street, Commissioners street, then the shore up to Pointe aux Trembles to link with the Montreal-Quebec highway.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise lor the first time may I add my humble words of congratulation to you, to your deputy and to the other officers who have been elected to high offices in this house. Permit me also to extend the heartiest congratulations to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I must confess that I cannot help but note that I have been placed in a rather peculiar position. The hon. gentlemen opposite are in fact with me, or beside me, or vice versa; the hon. gentlemen who are on my right are actually hon. gentlemen opposite, and the hon. gentlemen who are to my extreme right are to my left politically. However, from all this confusion I do hope that some clear-cut and definite proposals may be provided in order that the position of Canada and Canadians may be improved generally.
On this occasion I should like to describe briefly the constituency I represent, in order that hon. members may associate me with that part of Canada and so they may better understand the type of problems that arise and the solutions that may from time to time be proposed.
Mackenzie lies in the northwestern corner of the province of Saskatchewan. It is about 90 miles wide and approximately 600 miles long; in fact, in appearance it is like a miniature province of Saskatchewan. Its physical features too are very similar to those of the whole province of Saskatchewan, again on a miniature scale. The northern part of the constituency possesses an abundance of timber, lakes, rivers and rock formations that may in the near future prove to possess quantities of minerals. Recent activities in the vicinity of Hanson lake have added force to this view. In these areas are settlements where people make a living by fishing, trapping, mining in the area around Flin Flon and in the lumbering industry. Lumbering has always been an important source of income not only to those engaged directly m it but also to those farmers who have been able to supplement their income by finding employment during the winter months, which has helped to finance their farming operations.
You can well imagine the anxiety that was created when the The Pas Lumber Company had to curtail its operations and move to British Columbia. This was further aggravated by the announcement that the Saskatchewan timber board was to have suspended its operations in the town of Sturgis. However, we are very pleased with the recent announcement that a new blockboard (chipboard) factory is to be built in the vicinity of
[Mr. Lessard.)
the village of Arran. Recent surveys would indicate that there is a potential market on the prairies and also in certain areas of the United States that could be supplied where the saving in freight would make it more economical. It is hoped that this plant will provide considerable employment to many in that area. It may be of interest to the house to note that this plant is not a socialistic venture but a free enterprise endeavour.
I was rather amused the other day when the hon. member for Assiniboia said with reference to the election of March 31, as found on page 43 of Hansard of May 13:
A lot of people asked themselves: Should we not give the government a chance? Or, let's give John a chance.
Actually what a lot of people in my constituency were saying was, "Let's give the Prime Minister a chance to rid us of the socialists," for is it not true that farmers are the most individualistic and conservative people in Canada? Certainly they are not true socialists, for they love their independence; and if they did vote to give the Prime Minister a chance is it not an indication of the type of freedom-loving people we have in Canada? Did they not in the past send C.C.F representatives to the House of Commons to give them a chance to see what they could do? Is it not a credit to the people of Canada when they give recognition to a man who has done something for them, even though he had to do it in a short session of parliament?
For years, Mr. Speaker, we in the Mackenzie constituency, and I might say the people of Saskatchewan as a whole, have been wandering from one party to the other like an unwanted child drifting aimlessly from one foster parent to another, in the hope that one day we might be included in the family that now numbers ten. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we have now been adopted by the Conservative party which wants us, which needs us as much as we need it if we are to secure that unity and harmony that is as necessary for a party as it is for a home.
It was not without difficulty that we achieved this. This may be some consolation to the hon. member for Hull, who was so perturbed about Mr. Duplessis. I do not profess to be an authority on Mr. Duplessis, but I can assure the hon. member that we have had to work against a machine also. But unlike the wonderful one-horse chaise that ran for 100 years to a day, this machine ran for only 44 years before it collapsed. This is commonly known in the west as the Gardiner machine.
In my constituency of Mackenzie, where the majority of the people live in the southern

portion, their primary occupation being agriculture, we have some 50 towns and villages dependent on this industry. These people know in what position the Liberal administration placed them. They are certainly thankful to the previous Conservative administration for providing the price stabilization legislation.
These people are largely small farmers who have been carrying on diversified farming. Those who have been producing grain only are calculating the possibility of going into the production of cattle, hogs, sheep and poultry. No doubt they had these ideas before, but there was nothing to guide them under the former lackadaisical, sunbathing Liberal administration which preferred to argue its way out of a situation rather than do something about it. The price stabilization legislation will certainly be a guide to many farmers who can now be reasonably assured that they can produce other commodities without losing the shirt off their back if the market should drop at the end of a producing season.
Cash advances also provided many with money when they needed it. If they have not provided any more money than the farmer would have had ordinarily, they have certainly provided money when he needed it and thus relieved him of the stress and strain that comes with having commitments to meet but no money to do it with.
Businessmen across the country have nothing but praise for this legislation. It has meant that they have been able to collect many accounts where credit was advanced to such a point that they had to close their businesses because of lack of sufficient collateral. Too often I have seen businesses that have been developing for years suddenly come to a grinding halt, unable to carry on because of lack of funds in the hands of the farmers upon whom they depend. Businessmen will certainly be grateful for the small business section that is to be established for the purpose of investigating their needs.
Cash advances have been of assistance to local municipalities, where collections of taxes have improved, resulting in a saving in interest charges. Measures such as these have been needed for years. I am sorry to say they were not provided by the Liberal administration. Because of their lack there has been an effect on the small villages, towns and rural municipalities that may take years to correct.
Problems have been created in the wake. Many businesses have been closed and farmers have left their land. Many of these people have worked for years to develop their farms, their businesses and their homes. They have been forced to leave because of the economic pressure that has been
The Address-Mr. Korchinski applied to them. Many of these men and women have appeared on the labour market, and the effects of this are being felt today.
Behind them they have left depleted communities. Every year the population has dwindled. For example, in the small nine-township municipality where I have served as reeve for the past six years our population has dwindled from 2,200 in 1952 to 1,700 in 1957. I know communities that had eight or nine general stores and now have only three. Unlike communities that suffer from lack of services because of what may be termed growing pains, we have suffered from what I call an overdose of reducing pills.
Problems arise in such a situation because just as many services must be provided but fewer people are left to pay for them. Many of our country schools have had to be closed; in fact many small villages have had pressure applied to them to close their schools, and transportation has had to be arranged to larger centres. As a result many parents have found it more convenient to leave their children at these larger centres for the duration of the school term. This is a situation that is certainly unhealthy and unwise. Growing children do not have the guidance of their parents which is so necessary.
Briefly that is the situation that existed under the supposedly paternal guidance of the Liberal administration. Is it any wonder that we in the west rebelled against their fostering? Is it any wonder that there are no Liberal members from west of Ontario? The situation I have described is serious, one that deserves the deepest consideration of every member of the House of Commons. This situation has undoubtedly been caused by the farmer's inability to meet his day to day costs. Almost continually these costs have been mounting. In spite of the fact that the farmers have continually improved their techniques in order to become more and more economical and to reduce the cost of production, they have been waging a losing battle.
The people of my constituency will certainly be pleased to hear that payments from the barley pool will soon be made. Undoubtedly, they will be just as pleased if this government could see its way clear to making a similar announcement with regard to deficiency payments. I should like to urge the government to give careful consideration to these proposals in order that we may correct some of the existing situation. If we cannot completely eliminate this exodus from the farms and villages, then perhaps we can

It is encouraging to note that this government has been providing salesmanship in the marketing of our wheat. Indications are that in the period from August, 1957 to March, 1958, Canada has provided 36 per cent of the total world wheat marketings. This represents an increase of 11 per cent from the 25 per cent share of the world export market we enjoyed during the same period a year ago. If this is done many areas in my constituency will have almost completely disposed of their stock of grain. In an area such as the one I represent this statement would be true mainly because of two factors. First, many of the farmers in my area are small farmers who feed a lot of their grain and who only farm a half or three-quarters of a section. Second, the drought and hail damage experienced last year has left many farmers with very little grain.
This brings me to another point that was mentioned in the speech from the throne, and that is the pending changes in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Many inequities exist at the moment as a result of the administration of this act, and until such time as we can implement crop insurance the proposed changes will certainly be welcome.
Another provision mentioned in the throne speech that will certainly be heralded with joy is the proposed amendment to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. Many farmers are experiencing difficulty now in procuring such loans. These farmers go from year to year without improving their position because they are not in a financial position to purchase land when it becomes available or to increase their herd. Actually, they are left in a poorer position as their land becomes older and their machinery depleted. It has been my experience that assistance provided to veterans under the Veterans Land Act has worked fairly well. The majority of these veterans have been able to establish themselves and, because of the availability of credit, are doing fairly well. Something of a similar nature, without the delays experienced under that act, should be formulated for farmers generally.
I should like to take a moment to deal with that portion of the throne speech which mentions the government's plans for the development of the north. I do this because of the efforts of many opposition members to belittle this idea. I feel I must refer to it


since I represent a constituency that extends to the boundaries of the Northwest Territories and because of the statement made in the house by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin). On page 324 of Hansard for May 21, 1958 he said:
Along the line taken by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) I should like to assure them that in the north we get some lovely views of the northern lights and it is quite possible that their lack of success in the north could have been due to the fact that the good northern people may have mistaken this vision for just another example of these northern lights.
I should like to assure the hon. member that the good people of my constituency have captured that vision of the north. In fact, they caught that vision so well that they recorded a plurality in my favour over both the C.C.F. and Liberal candidates, and they were both honourable and respected gentlemen. The result has left many C.C.F. and Liberals bewildered. I hope, that while they are star-gazing, the dawn of development will soon appear for them. The people of my constituency have certainly caught the vision of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). They have seen their constituency neglected for too long to by-pass the opportunity afforded them. It is only through such a policy of development as was mentioned in the throne speech that roads such as the Hanson road and the Otosquen road will be provided so that access may be gained to the timber and mineral resources. My people are patiently awaiting the time when a second trans-Canada highway will one day cross their constituency, bringing with it a tourist trade. My constituents are certainly aware of the financial assistance that will be provided to the provinces for these much needed developments. This, in turn, should leave the provinces in a sounder financial position to provide assistance for schools, local roads and hospitals. Assistance of this type should provide relief from the heavy burden of taxes which have already reached the saturation point.
The people I represent are looking forward to the employment that will be provided by such projects as the South Saskatchewan dam. If these people find that they must seek employment, then they will appreciate finding this employment in an area near their homes. When these projects are undertaken, they will certainly revitalize the communities that have degenerated in the last few years. My constituents have certainly seen that vision, and it has given them hope. It is this same hope that has been registered in all of Canada and has brought about a unity of purpose unequalled in the history of Canada. This unity will be strengthened by the bill of rights that will be introduced this session. Although we in Canada have enjoyed a

measure of freedom which has been equalled by no others, the religious and ethnic groups will undoubtedly welcome this measure as a great victory for them. It will no doubt provide them with a measure of comfort to know that nothing short of a complete revolution could take away these freedoms.
Canada is a proud nation and we, as Canadians, are proud of our ancestry, whatever it may be. The two great races that helped to mould this nation into one which is jealously viewed by others not enjoying such a measure of freedom and independence, must certainly be proud. They have displayed a degree of tolerance and understanding that serves as a fine example to the rest of the world. With this same understanding we, as members of parliament, should go forward to build a better Canada, to build a better world. I am sure my constituents will agree with that.

Mr. Speaker, it is with the greatest of humility that I rise to address this house. First, I should like to congratulate you upon your election to the high post which you now hold. I am sure, judging by what I have seen and heard in this house, that every member will receive a fair hearing. I should like also to congratulate the deputy speaker and chairman as well as the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have nothing but praise to offer these two gentlemen. I have listened to many speakers over the past days hoping to learn something of Canada and its problems. I am sorry that I am not bilingual for I should certainly like to acquaint myself with the problems and the good points of that part of the country from which these French-speaking members come.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to tell you about the constituency which I represent. It is said that the constituency of Cariboo is the third largest in Canada. It has two cities and numerous small towns, the largest city being Prince George at the junction of the Fraser and Nechaki rivers. The chief industry in the area surrounding Prince George is lumbering. There are 600 sawmills there and enough lumber is piled up in the area surrounding Prince George to build a city as large as Edmonton. Farming and cattlefeeding play no small part in the economy of this section of the country. In the town of Quesnel on the Fraser river there is a plywood plant employing 400 workers. The Prince George planing mill gives employment to thousands of mill hands. Since this constituency is at the mouth of the Rocky mountain trench, great things are expected
The Address-Mr. Henderson when the Wenner-Gren plan gets into its stride. McBride is another centre some 80 miles east devoted to dairying and the growing of grass seeds.
This vast country is rich in minerals and oil at Fort St. John, on the banks of the mighty Peace river, which is a hustling young city. Here there are gas and oil wells stretching north from Fort St. John 500 miles to the Fort Nelson country on the river. Then on to the Lower Post, about 300 miles, this country is serviced by the famous Alaska highway which is no doubt the best and greatest gravelled highway on the North American continent. This country consists of mighty valleys so large that a country the size of Belgium could be dropped into one of them. The Alaska highway goes on into the Yukon. A range of mountains borders this land which abounds with game such as mountain goats, sheep, deer and bear. West to Quesnel we come to the ranching country and its mighty ranches. In that part of Canada we have much larger ranches than the much publicized ranches of Texas.
From Fort St. John you follow the Peace river west to Hudson Hope. There big interests are drilling for footings at the Rocky Mountain canyon. This canyon carries the river through a pass cut through the rocks. These rock walls are immense in height and you can hear the river rushing through the canyon for five miles. It is proposed to harness this river at this point to supply electricity to the city of Vancouver.
Surrounding Hudson Hope are numerous cattle ranches and farms growing alfalfa. A range of mountains divides my constituency, cutting it right down the middle. The state of New York could be placed between the Prince George area and the Dawson Creek area. Dawson Creek is the largest shipping point for grain in the British commonwealth. In the speech from the throne mention is made of the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake. I believe this railway should commence from Dawson Creek to Great Slave lake where it would pass over an immense body of iron ore at Hines Creek.
That part of the constituency which I have just mentioned consists of one of the finest farming areas in Canada. Mixed farming is the order of the day. The feeding of cattle is taking place on many farms and with the price of beef up there is bound to be an increase in the number of cattle being fed. Large acreages are being devoted to the growing of grass seeds. At present the kind most cultivated are Merion blue grass, creeping red fescue, brome grass and various clovers. Across the Peace river there is a large acreage devoted to the growing of wheat,

The Address-Mr. Ormiston flax, barley and oats. This land is being farmed in blocks of 1,000 to 2,000 acres and is really an empire in its own right.
The pipe line carrying gas to the coast runs through this district, coming from the wells at Taylor 20 miles west. The country has hundreds of oil wells as far north as Nelson. At Taylor, there is a large scrubbing plant. It is estimated that thousands of tons of sulphur will be shipped to the coast via the P.G.E. The railway will carry grain, lumber and livestock to the coast.
I think I have told you enough about this wonderful country which I represent. Under the leadership of our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) this riding will again come into its heritage. After 23 years of inactivity under the Liberal government, we are now headed in the right direction. We now have a leader who has the understanding of the common people.
I was very pleased to hear in the speech from the throne about the housing program. In my constituency, as I have mentioned previously, we have enough lumber piled up to build a city the size of Edmonton.
I should like to see pensions raised, as the recipients of these would put the money received right back into circulation.
I should like to see the federal government assist in the cost of education. I know whereof I speak as I am, and have been chairman of school district No. 59 in British Columbia for some time. With a birthrate in my constituency higher than that in Delhi, India, we are having difficulty building enough schools.
The grain advances were certainly welcome and showed that the government is going to help the farmer and I believe that the P.F.A.A. should be amended. I am sure that with our present Prime Minister at the helm the Conservative government ship will sail into the sea of prosperity and good times.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a proud privilege to represent one's country in the councils of the nation. As one rises in this great chamber one feels an air of awe, inspired I suppose by those who have preceded us, men and women who have come here, by the democratic process, to make their contribution. Here, indeed, Mr. Speaker, is where the history of our great country has been written. Great men, inspired no doubt to carve their niches in the hall of fame, have set a standard for us to follow. They have played their full part in the onward march of civilization; they have handed to us a great trust, a great heritage. These builders of Canada, the Macdonalds, the Cartiers, the Lauriers, the Bordens and


the Meighens, all have played their full part. They are the mountain summits in the paths of human progress. We honour such men wherever we find them and we feel keenly their loss. One remains among us. I am thinking of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen whose keen and analytical mind sought to find a greater destiny for our beloved country. In spite of what has gone before, we have not yet reached the crossroads; indeed, we seem but to have reached the beginning. Inspired by our great leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) I am sure we are on the threshold of a new and greater adventure in nation building.
This party, this government, I am sure is not going to view Canada in retrospect, except as a guidepost, but we are looking to the distant horizons, to our great hinterland, to the rich treasure which is indeed a challenge to our imagination. Provided with the type of leadership we now enjoy, I am sure Canada will go forward to attain her great destiny.
Millions will come to our shores to share our vast development and native Canadians will share the rich reward that beckons our best pioneering instincts. Speaking of the pioneers, I am not unmindful of our early beginning. I am deeply conscious of those who came to Canada in our early years. They did not seek any easy existence. They faced a great challenge. They accepted their lot and in Ontario and Quebec there was hewed from the virgin forest the beginning. They laid the foundation upon which future generations were to erect a superstructure, substantial in its parts and honourable to its builders. It is worthy of note that we have not failed. Constantly the march forward went on. In two tragic wars this nation gave a full account of itself. It is true that we paid a terrific price. More than 100,000 of our best and bravest lie buried under foreign soil-the lost generation-but they have written lines that will never fade from the brightest pages in Canadian history.
Came the opening of the great Northwest commonly referred to about the turn of the century. With the division of it into provinces in 1905, organized society turned earnestly to the development of this vast western domain. It is not necessary to repeat here mention of the contributions we as westerners have made to the national welfare. Certainly we stimulated activity in the east. Indeed we provided them with the incentive and markets to become a great industrial empire and there has been produced from those western lands billions upon billions of dollars in wealth.
Saskatchewan, my own great province, became recognized as the bread basket of the empire. We now realize that was but the

beginning. These prairies are again going to share with our sister provinces that wealth referred to as black gold by many. In addition there is our natural gas which is now being piped east to improve the productive and industrial capacity of Ontario and Quebec. However, that is as it should be, as far as I am concerned. Let us share our rich treasure. Let us weld ourselves into one great nation. Indeed, let us grow richer together. Yet in growing richer together we must not overlook the fact that while we all recognize that no one section can become richer by making some other part of the nation poorer, we on the plains do not want to be neglected.
That is the vision which captured the imagination of my people; the program, the policy enunciated by my right hon. leader fascinated the western people. Today they look forward with new hope, conscious of the fact that when this government creates, as I am sure it will, the right atmosphere, nothing can hold us back. Westerners are resourceful-of necessity they must be-and, given the incentive and leadership, we will all have cause to view with satisfaction the results of our efforts.
A word now about my own constituency and, incidentally, my principal concern. In June 1957 the pattern was set; by March of this year the rout was surely evident. My right hon. opponent, who had sat in this house since 1935, failed to detect it; indeed, when he issued his manifesto, and I say this with great respect for one for whom I have the greatest regard as a public servant, he said he would like to return to Ottawa to witness the completion of the South Saskatchewan river dam. He, having toyed with this great development for 20 years, prompted some of my speakers to suggest that the dam was not going to be built in Ottawa and that if he wanted to witness the completion of the dam then the best place for him to view the results was right from his lofty perch in Saskatchewan. I presume that my right hon. friend the former minister of agriculture -sometimes also referred to as the minister of elections-will have a good view of the work in connection with this mammoth project, the completion of which we believe will add greatly to the wealth and resources of my province.
The constituency of Melville, which I have the honour to represent, is made up of the best Canadians. I am proud to represent them here and, while I want to play my full part, I am sure I will not be misunderstood if I appear to keep the needs of Melville constantly before me and in particular the problems of western farmers.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, as a new member of this house I should like to offer to you my congratulations on your election to the office you now hold.
The aim and purpose of the Conservative government, as I see it, is to provide a fair and equal opportunity for all, regardless of differences in religious and racial backgrounds, or position, and of age. This means that we must remember Canadians are no longer just the descendants of a particular nationality. From the fishing banks of Newfoundland to the shores of Vancouver island, Canada is filled with composite Canadians, a product achieved by taking a dozen or

The Address-Mr. Skoreyko more nationalities and mixing them in a pot steaming with ambition, vigour and vision. This product is a real Canadian, with a nationality of his own; a mixture of those people who in countless numbers have emigrated over the decades from Germany, France, the Ukraine, Poland, Holland, Sweden, China and England, to take up their futures in Canada and to offer their faith and their various abilities towards the building of a great nation. It is the mixture of those nationalities which has made possible the diversified disposition of this country's economy. It is people like these who have made this country of ours a proud nation.
Canada has possibly the greatest potential for prosperity and development of any country in the world. We have here in our country more area, more mineral resources, more power resources and more agricultural resources than even the United States. Only Russia can equal our potentiality, but Russia, with its regimentation, does not have the free enterprise which is the incentive for creative thinking in the development of a nation. What greater challenge could we ask of our country? It is the challenge being offered to Canadians by the Conservative government, a challenge born of vision of what the Canada of tomorrow can and will be if we plan and work at this time to bring it about. It is the vision of a country which dates back to the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, the great architect of confederation, who dreamed of joining the scattered provinces and promoting the development of the west. They scoffed at Sir John's proposals; a railway, they said, from wigwam to wigwam. Sir John's administration had the last laugh in his day, and without his rail line what would have been the development of the western provinces today?
Today the opposition, parroting its 19th century predecessors, jeeringly refer to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker's) vision as being only connecting links from igloo to igloo. The Conservatives will have the last laugh in this project also, for these igloos which we will connect up will some day be the foundations for thriving communities, processing plants and refineries. This is all part of the vision of our government, the opening up of our vast northlands and the utilization of the equally vast natural resources of this area.
If our natural resources,-wherever they may be found, in the Northwest Territories, the western provinces, the Atlantic provinces or in old Ontario and Quebec-are developed with vision and vigour, then the general

level of prosperity for all Canadians will be raised to new and appreciable heights. The development of these resources as part of our Canada first policy must be immediately proceeded with if Canadians of this and the next generations are to reap the rightful benefits from the tremendous treasure chest which is Canada. While precious time has already been wasted under previous government administration, we can with hard work look to the fulfilment in our own time of the dreams of those Canadians of yesterday who laid the foundations of this dominion from sea to sea.
It is a policy that puts Canada first, and it is time we put Canada first in our administration, trade policies and foreign affairs. For years now Canada has been suffering increased losses of Canadian business ownership to the United States. We have been selling outright many of our natural resources to foreign powers whose interests are not always the same as ours. The investment is necessary to our growth, but it can go too far. Increasing control by Americans, or any other nation, in Canadian business can rob us of our economic and even our political independence. We must start now to provide measures to prevent such a collapse of our independence. We must start now to develop Canada for Canadians and by Canadians. We believe that such development cannot be left to domestic or foreign private capital alone, but must be stimulated and encouraged by government action.
Our present plans for a second trans-Canada highway from Winnipeg west to Edmonton and Jasper and through the Yellowhead route would shorten by many miles the distance between points in the northern part of the four western provinces to the west coast. Such a road would also be a very excellent military highway from eastern points to Edmonton which is such an important military centre and the gateway to the north.
I represent the constituency of Edmonton East which I believe is the only entirely urban federal constituency in Alberta. This is the constituency that in the outside world gains importance from the fact that it contains Clarke stadium which our Edmonton Eskimos football team calls home. My constituency contains five meat packing plants that process a big precentage of meats sold in northern Alberta and a great deal which is exported. Edmonton East also contains many other manufacturing plants as well as many of the finest residential communities in the city.
I might comment that the extension of unemployment insurance benefits and the further allocation of funds under the National

Housing Act, passed by this house, is of great importance to the working people of my constituency.
May I conclude by saying for the record that I was elected by my constituents because they felt that I could do a job for them and for Canada as a whole in this government. I will work as hard as I can for the people of Edmonton East and for the unity of this great country so that I may be deserving of the confidence they have placed in me.

Mr. Speaker, this being the first time that I rise to address the house, and as I represent a constituency made up of practically equal parts of French-speaking and English-speaking electors, I shall begin my remarks in my mother tongue.
I first wish to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, and to tell you how impressed I have been by the way in which you preside over the sittings of this house.
I also congratulate the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Sevigny) and the deputy chairman (Mr. Rea), as well as the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. (Text):
My first duty, Mr. Speaker, is to thank the electors of the constituency of St. Boniface who have chosen me to represent them and I want to assure them I will do all in my power to prove worthy of their confidence. I pray that I shall never be backward in defending their interests and that I may do so in a most effective manner.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to all the previous speakers, those government members on both sides of the house and members of the opposition who sit on the righthand corner of this chamber. In my opinion all subjects and matters mentioned in the speech from the throne have been adequately covered. There is one subject, however, which while given prominence in the throne speech has not been discussed overmuch and it is that part of the speech from the throne that reads as follows:
My government will continue to make unremitting effort to assist the peaceful solution of international problems and in the accomplishment by patient negotiation of a substantial measure of disarmament.
To me this subject is the most important with which this government can deal. It was touched upon last evening by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who referred to a speech made by Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery on his recent visit to Canada as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 15 under the headline "Montgomery
The Address-Mr. Regnier Feels Canada Should Lead Free Crusade" and I quote from that report:
It seems to me Canada is in a unique position to provide robust world leadership. Your nation cannot be charged with the stigma of colonialism: you're lucky that way. You have a very good amalgam of French and British blood; that's good. It is quite clear to me that the nations of the world are looking to Canada for a lead. That is a fact. I am not saying that to please you. I would like to see Canada develop a foreign policy of its own, not tacked on to someone else, and give that lead.
The reference by the hero of El Alamein to the fact that Canada cannot be charged with the stigma of colonialism brings to my mind the first two letters I received after March 31, one in English and one in French, which I would like to read. The first, in English, dated April 2, 1958, is addressed to myself and reads as follows:
In view of the last elections, I salute you with my felicitations. I also would like to emphasize a subject of great importance which has already been overlooked' much too often and too long.
In my belief a flag is to a country like a cross is to a church. A country can't very well hold its proper place behind its mother's skirt, which some pretend England still is to us. A flag also represents the right to talk more freely in world matters.
I'm sure you know the importance of this matter as do many of us, but have been somehow afraid to insult or hurt England. I respect England very much but I think it is time to leave England like it is time for a 25-year old man to leave his mother to lead his own life. We could stay very close to England just the same.
I leave you with this thought which I know as a good citizen and a good M.P. you won't overlook.
I will not reveal the name of the man who wrote the letter as I do not have the authority to do so. The other letter which bears the same date is in French and deals with approximately the same matter. It reads as follows:
(Translation):
I believe you deserve congratulations on the results of the elections. I hope that the Conservative party will lead Canada on the road to progress and help it attain its rightful place in the world.
I should like to speak to you about a matter which I consider quite important if we want to make Canada a better country. I doubt if there is anybody in this country who, while claiming to be a patriot, is opposed to a distinctive Canadian flag. It is high time for Canada to realize that it is a nation in its own right and not a colony, as many distant countries must think.
This would be no insult to England and Canada could still play a very active role in the commonwealth, as was demonstrated by Asian and African countries which take pride in having their own flag.
With the decisive majority you have in parliament, there should be no great difficulty in undertaking a survey to decide what the majority of people think, in schools, in universities, in the streets.
Sincerely-
(Text):
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, a distinctive flag should be an element of greater unity in

The Address-Mr. Regnier Canada and not one of division. Perhaps the delay in choosing a distinctive flag has been the fear that it might create division. In my humble opinion this country is now ready and anxious to let the world know what has been a fact for a long time, that we have achieved full nationhood. The people of Canada are ready for this. I believe the adoption of a national flag would give us a greater voice in international affairs. A flag is a symbol but it represents the true independence of a nation and the voice of this country cannot carry its full weight unless the fact of our independence becomes universally known.
In the election campaign in my constituency we did not make this an issue, and I do not believe it should be an issue of party politics. It should be something that all parties are more or less unanimous about before we can achieve that aim. I hope that under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) we shall attain this final objective.
I have heard in this house many discussions regarding who was entitled to the greatest credit for obtaining Canadian autonomy.
I have heard some speakers say it was Sir Robert Borden who was the first Canadian to sign Canada's name on the Treaty of Versailles. I believe Ernest Lapointe signed in Washington on behalf of Canada a treaty connected with fisheries. I think the honour as to working for Canadian autonomy and the glory is divided pretty well equally between the parties in this house. I believe we should all work as patriots to achieve full nationhood, which is a fact, but we still need a symbol.
Before closing, I should like to bring to the attention of the house the fact that the city of St. Boniface will on June 16 celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of its foundation. I know I do not need to talk about the history of St. Boniface. St. Boniface has played a great roll in the history of Canada. In St. Boniface we have the first church established in the great northwest, the first college and the first school. It is really the cradle of civilization in the west. It is the capital of French culture and the largest French speaking city west of the Ottawa river. I could say a lot more but I do not wish to take up the time of the house. However, I should like to quote a few verses from a poem "The Red River Voy-ageur", by John G. Whittier, who has immortalized the St. Boniface cathedral:
The voyageur smiles as he listens To the sound that grows apace;
Well he knows the vesper ringing Of the bells of St. Boniface.

The bells of the Roman Mission
That call from their turrets twain,
To the boatman on the river
To the hunter on the plain!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed, after so many hon. members, to congratulate you on your re-election to the post of Speaker of the house. I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) on his appointment to the post of Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees, as well as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) who has been elected deputy chairman of committees.
I would also like to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielson) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne as well as the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) whom the right hon. minister has been pleased to appoint respectively to the portfolio of National Defence and to the Secretary of State Department at the very outset of this session.
I congratulate them with all my heart. I wish their administration every success and I am assured that they will obtain in this regard the co-operation of all their colleagues in this house.
There is one promise which has already been kept by the Prime Minister. The province of Quebec now has five ministers and has been promised one more.
You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that in 1942, from May 11 to October 7, that is to say for five months, the province of Quebec had only one French-speaking minister to represent it, and that was the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. Yet, in 1941, my province had given the federal Liberal government 64 members from Quebec out of a possible total of 65. On the other hand, when the Progressive Conservative party was elected on June 10, 1957, having gained at that time only 9 Quebec Conservative members, the Prime Minister immediately appointed three ministers from the province of Quebec. That is why the electors of the constituency of Rich-mond-Wolfe decided to show the Prime Minister the admiration and consideration they have for him by giving him a Conservative member to represent them in the House of Commons and, accordingly, contributing to the great victory of March 31 last.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I should now like to outline to the house the situation and the needs of my constituency. My constituency is made up of two main groups of people: workers and farmers. If the city of Sherbrooke is considered as the queen of the eastern townships, the constituency of Rich-

mond-Wolfe is considered as one of the finest parts of the eastern townships area, because of its lakes, its rivers, the St. Francis river running through its whole breadth, its many mountains which delight the visitors, its agriculture which shows that the Canadian is still attached to the soil, and its varied industries which provide jobs, not only for workers of their factories, but also for those who supply those industries.
That is why the workers of my constituency were very happy to learn that unemployment insurance benefits had been extended up to June 28 next.
There we have one way of bringing immediate relief to the unemployed. However, the working class of my riding of Richmond-Wolfe want more than unemployment insurance benefits. They want jobs.
They therefore welcome the amendment to the National Housing Act raising from $400 to $750 million the total amount made available to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in 1958. Construction being the yardstick of a country's activities and prosperity, we hope that this first undertaking will mean jobs for as many workers as possible and that by the end of 1958 more Canadians will own their own home.
However, on behalf of those who will remain unemployed, I ask that some very important public works be carried out in my constituency. The St. Francis river, at flood time, causes considerable damage and even loss of life. I wish to remind my fellow members of the sad events which occurred at Bromptonville in 1948 when the St. Francis river overflowed its banks and swept away more than 10 houses, with some loss of life. Other municipalities, such as Greenlay, and Richmond, suffer heavy damage every year, sometimes more than once in a single year, by overflowing. On behalf of all these municipalities, I draw to the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and of all the hon. members the need for a retaining wall in strategic places so as to obviate the great dangers of loss of life and damage to property.
Among the public works which could be undertaken to stop unemployment, I could mention the construction of a post office at Bromptonville. It would be a magnificent opportunity to commemorate with the population of that town the centenary of the celebration of the first mass. Impressive ceremonies took place there on Sunday May 25th last.
The Address-Mr. Dubois
While providing that little municipality with a government building and giving jobs to its workers, this would leave another memory which that fine population would not fail to recall on great occasions.
Mr. Speaker, the city of Asbestos is the centre of the Richmond-Wolfe riding. It has the largest asbestos mines in the world. It also has the world's largest mill, capable of processing close to 20,000 tons of ore daily. However the city has special needs of prime importance. Although it has 11,000 inhabitants, it is located five miles from the railway. It is therefore deprived of services essential to its greater development. Besides needing a larger unemployment insurance office, it urgently needs a customs office and a telegraph service which would be very beneficial to the population of that constituency.
Another project which would help alleviate unemployment would be to build an armoury at Asbestos. Sherbrooke, Drummondville, Victoriaville have their armouries, but Asbestos has none. This would therefore be a wonderful opportunity to put the unemployed to work in my constituency. Besides those unemployed young men would be glad to spend their spare time acquiring a training that would stand them in good stead and take their minds off the hard times they are going through.
Still in the public works field, there is the matter of level crossings, most of which afford no security at all to the people of my constituency. In the town of Richmond, alone, there are two very dangerous locations which should be attended to, either by putting up signal lights, or building an overpass.
In Danville there is a CNR viaduct, but this is now obsolete, being too narrow, and it should be rebuilt so as to assure that city of all the required safety on its highway network linking Asbestos to all great highways. In Weedon too, there is a pressing need for civilian protection in the form of warning lights at the level crossing on Main street.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) impressively outlined the sad plight of the textile industry, stating its numerous problems and suggesting various means which could improve it both in the eastern townships as elsewhere in Canada. Other hon. members also attempted to speak up and state the case of that industry but nobody as yet has referred to the precarious position of the seamless and full-fashioned hosiery industry.

The Address-Mr. Dubois
There are any number of constituencies in Canada-and I have some in my constituency, more exactly in the town of Richmond- which are bound to disappear completely if the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government do not take action soon.
At the present time we have imports of full fashioned and seamless hosiery from the United States. When these goods pass through customs, exporters and importers claim valuation on them at rates applying to industrial waste of little value. This hosiery which is neither dyed nor pressed, and not yet prepared for commercial merchandising, escapes the attention of the officers and is assessed as practically worthless merchandise whereas it is in fact first quality merchandise. This is unfair competition for the Canadian full fashioned hose and seamless hose industry. It must moreover be noted that because of this devious process, not only does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) fail to collect the difference between the extremely low rates involved and a proper valuation, as I have pointed out, but he also fails to collect the 10 per cent excise tax. Industry has gradually slowed down and there is growing unemployment not only in that town but in every other town with a similar industry.
Once the ailment has been diagnosed and is known, appropriate remedies must be applied as soon as possible.
These remedies, Mr. Speaker, I now make so bold as to put before the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) so that this full fashioned hose and seamless hose industry may continue its activity as it has in the past.
1.	There should only be a few ports of entry allowed for full fashioned hose and seamless hose so that the Canadian importers of those products may be subjected to rigid controls.
2.	In these customs offices, there should be appointed at least one officer who is an expert judge of full fashioned and seamless hose so that proper valuation may be put on the product and duty may be collected on that correct valuation, plus the 10 per cent excise tax.
Customs tariffs should be modified so as to apply to the weight and not the number of dozens as now indicated on entry bills.
I humbly submit those few suggestions to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
[Mr. Dubois.)
Mr. Speaker, the farmers of my riding of Richmond-Wolfe welcome the setting up of a Farm Price Stabilization Board. The farmer now has a brighter outlook on life and now wants to establish his sons on the land, instead of letting them desert the farm and swell the ranks of unemployed in the cities. I shall not labour this point because the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) has very ably described the benefits the Conservative government has awarded the farmers throughout Canada since it took over on June 10, 1957. There is, however, a point which is peculiar to my riding. The rural population are mainly dairy farmers, and this kind of farming is their principal source of income. They must therefore find a market for their produce. They can, of course sell to dairies, but this is not a sufficient market for all the milk they produce. For this reason they are now asking for a cheese factory not like those formerly operating on every country road and manufacturing a product that did not always comply with existing regulations, but a central cheese factory with modern equipment conforming with the specifications of the Department of Agriculture.
While helping the farmers of my constituency, this would cut down unemployment during the building of this industry and afterwards favour competition with the big companies that exploit the farmers of my constituency.
Since every farmer has a woodlot on his farm, he wants to work it, but expects a reasonable return. Accordingly, farmers of my constituency have urged me to ask the house and the price stabilization board to set a price in advance for the next cutting season of pulpwood. I therefore submit their request to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) so that all farmers, not only of my constituency but throughout the district, may benefit from a fair and reasonable price.
I should now like, Mr. Speaker, to move beyond the limits of my constituency and consider all Canadians of my country. I would like to deal with the question of obscene literature. On Saturday, May 17 last, before a meeting of the Quebec union of municipalities, in Hull, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) made a speech which indicated that he intends to put an end to this wave of immorality sweeping over all Canada. It is a highly deplorable situation which prevents civic authorities from doing what they would like to punish those who spread

or publish this trash. The Minister of Justice is aware of the danger this represents, as shown by his words as reported by the newspaper La Presse:
The problem, as I understand it, concerns mainly the youth of our country. I am very much afraid that, if we let this flow of degrading and salacious literature be sold openly on newsstands, without any hindrance we risk losing a whole generation.
To show his great determination to correct that evil and to give support and encouragement to all those who fight against that obscene literature, he added:
We are also considering whether the criminal code should not be amended to include a summary procedure such as now obtains in Great Britain and under which a newsdealer may be summoned to show cause why an order of the court providing for the destruction of the alleged obscene publication found in his premises should not be executed.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Minister of Justice will have every possibility to give the Canadian people a clear and accurate definition of the word "obscenity''. I also congratulate him on a very important and magnificent speech.
Mr. Speaker, last fall the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) increased some social security benefits, such as the pensions for the aged, the needy, the blind and war veterans. This was most welcome by these people who thereby were given a new lease on life, after years of destitution due to the high cost of living. It took a Conservative government to realize this deplorable situation and to put an end to it.
However, would it not be possible now to increase family allowances to the highest possible level so as to give parents an opportunity to provide their children with the necessities of life? Moreover, if family allowances were extended to age 18 for children still attending school, parents would be in a position to give their children a much more complete education. However the allowances should be geared to the cost of living and be raised to a level which would allow parents to fulfil their great responsibilities when children decide to seek higher education. A sound distribution in this field would certainly help develop talents and give Canada the skilled people we need.
On Monday May 20, I heard the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) speak about a national flag. He must be unaware that the Liberal party never wanted to give the Canadian people a distinctive national flag. The Liberals were in office for 22 years and in that time received thousands of petitions, requests and resolutions asking for a distinctive national flag; yet they never found a way to provide the Canadian people with

The Address-Mr. Kindt such a flag. However, another government, which has only been in power since June 10, 1957, recognizing that Canada is made up of two great races, that there are also two official languages, French and English, recognized by the constitution of 1867 took action and immediately recognized bilingualism in the parliamentary restaurant. Moreover, as outlined in the speech from the throne, it is going to introduce a measure providing for the installation of a system of simultaneous translation of the debates. Such positive action is but a hint of what can be expected from the Conservative government that will provide Canada and the whole Canadian people with a distinctive national flag.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding the first speech I have the honour to deliver in the House of Commons, it is my pleasure to express to every hon. member the appreciation and congratulations of all the electors of my riding. I thank them for the mark of confidence they gave me on the day of my victory. They can rest assured that with a Conservative government and a leader such as the right hon. Prime Minister, Canada will grow, prosperity will come back, and the national unity so well advocated by the right hon. Prime Minister will make Canada the greatest country in the eyes of all the peoples of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer my congratulations to you on your re-election as Speaker of this house. I should like also to congratulate the Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman on their election to posts of trust and responsibility. Following the precedent set by those who have preceded me in this debate, I should like to commend the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Neilsen) for their contribution to this throne speech debate.
I have the honour of representing the Macleod riding in this house. This constituency sent its first representative to the House of Commons in 1908, just 50 years ago, and that representative was a Conservative, Mr. John Herron. I mention this to indicate that my constituency is fundamentally Progressive Conservative because it started out that way.
I hasten to say, however, that out of the past 37 years the constituency has been represented for 14 years by a farmer representative and during the last 23 years by a Social

The Address-Mr. Kindt Credit representative, the Rev. E. G. Hansell. On March 31 the people of the Macleod riding reverted to their former tradition and elected me a Progressive Conservative to this House of Commons with the largest majority that has ever been given a member for that riding.
I am grateful to the people of the Macleod constituency for having elected me as their representative. I should say, in addition, that they felt it was time to return to the two-party system. I appreciate the support I received from people in all walks of life.
It is the custom in this house to say a few words about one's constituency, and particularly the problems which confront the people there. It is necessary to do this on a regional basis and to delineate the different areas in order to bring out particular problems. For instance, there is the Crowsnest area, a region which is familiar to most people in this house. There we have the tremendous coal deposits and coal mines which are experiencing some trouble in finding markets. As a result of the competition from oil, gas and electricity, as well as other competing sources of energy, the demand for coal has gone down so that the mines are finding it extremely difficult to obtain sufficient orders to enable them to remain in existence. As a matter of fact, last week the mine at Bellevue in Alberta was closed, putting approximately 150 people out of employment. I must say how sorry I am, and I am sure I speak on behalf of the government, to see this particular mine closed. I hope that some measures can be taken which will alleviate the hardships these miners are facing as a result of the closing of this mine.
I want to compliment the government on the efforts which they have made to try to find a market for coal. Last July an order in council was passed opening the Japanese market for coal. We had hoped that this step might help with respect to demand for coal in western Canada. I can say that some 50,000 tons of coal were shipped last fall to Japan from Canmore and
2,000	tons were shipped from Coleman. That was a big help. Since then another 50,000 tons are on order from Canmore and 1,000 tons from Coleman. But coal orders are dependent upon the demand from the Japanese. If the steel industries of Japan are in trouble we cannot expect coal orders which will be of a continuing nature or at least of such regularity that the coal miners of Alberta can depend on them as their chief

market for their coal. In other words, despite all that the government has done in the way of subventions it looks as though we are in trouble in the west in so far as the coal mining industry is concerned. Anything which this government can do will, I am sure, be greatly appreciated by those people engaged in the coal mining industry in the west.

I am glad to hear that. Turning to other problems of the Macleod constituency, may I say that we have there the Turner valley oil and natural gas area. As you know, that was among the first oil and natural gas fields to be discovered in western Canada. We also have the Flat Top mountain and Savana creek area and the Fincher creek field from which natural gas will be flowing to the homes of Ontario in the not too distant future when the trans-Canada pipe line has been completed.
These tremendous sources of energy-I refer to coal, natural gas, oil, hydro electric and others-raise serious problems which the people of western Canada are anxious to have solved. The solution of these problems rests with the execution of a national development policy which will help in their development. One of the big problems of the oil industry and the natural gas industry is that of finding markets. As you know, when natural gas comes from the ground, only about 10 per cent of the total production, is dry methane gas. That is the kind of gas which is put through the mains. The other 90 per cent is wet gas. It is necessary to scrub this gas and separate the methane, ethane, propane,

butane and sulphur dioxide, all of which aside from methane are byproducts which must find a market. That consideration brings up the question of the establishment and economic development of means for the utilization of these byproducts. By that I mean the development of petrochemical industries throughout western Canada to utilize these natural resources. As you may know, some
10,000	products are produced from these petrochemical industries, and those products are all capable of being produced from the source of the hydrocarbons which are available in the Macleod riding.
I come now to one other large industry which flourishes in the Macleod riding. I would be remiss, if I did not call your attention to the cattle ranching industry. Along the foothills area east of the Rocky mountains the cattle ranching industry of western Canada is largely located. I should say that roughly 75 per cent of the big cattle outfits of western Canada are located in that region. For instance, there is the Bar-U ranch which was started many years ago by George Lane; there is also the Prince of Wales ranch and many others. I should like to pay my compliments to the government on behalf of the stockmen of western Canada for their policies in keeping the United States market open and available to Canadian cattle. It has been greatly appreciated by producers and feeders. May I add that they would desire that, in so far as possible, this government pursue policies whereby they may have the advantage of that United States market.
Turning to grain farming, as you proceed east from the foothills area of the Rocky mountains you get into a relatively level area extending for well over 100 miles in the Macleod riding where wheat is the predominant crop. When we come to consider economic cycles with respect to wheat and farming, may I say that the farm cycle turned down in 1951. It has been down for seven years. This cycle is different from the general cycle. Hence wheat farmers in my constituency have been in difficulties for the past four or five years. May I say that they are anxious that, whatever is done in the way of programs which affect their industry, those programs may have at the centre the question of price. In other words, the farmer is out there to make money. He is interested in price. He is of course also interested in his farm as a way of life. He would like to see a well-rounded co-ordinated program that includes price stabilization, conservation, adequate farm credit, et cetera, which will give to him his fair share of the national income. I shall have more to say on this subject when the estimates are under discussion.
The Address-Mr. Taylor
