The visitors will find that a physical revolution is taking place; new industrial cities like Kitimat have sprung up; oil and gas have transformed the quiet farms behind the mountains to the east; surveyors are swarming through the great Rocky mountain trench; to the south the railway builders and the road builders are stitching the province together.
Hon. members who visit British Columbia will also find that it is still that part of Canada where nothing is done by halves, where in every field-in politics and art, in climate and geography and in ethnic make-up -the pendulum swings abruptly and unpredictably from one extreme to the other. It is the all or nothing province, the Texas and at the same time the California of Canada.
I would fail my constituents if I did not take this opportunity to particularly invite to British Columbia this summer the hon. members on the treasury benches. It is so important to me and to my constituents that they grasp the compelling issues in British Columbia. This province, for instance, has the largest percentage of old people in Canada, and also the largest percentage of young married couples; it has the most marriages per capita and the most divorces; the most advanced prison system and the most crime; some of the best social services and some of the worst delinquency; there are proportionately more newcomers in British Columbia than in any other province and, unfortunately, more drug addicts. It is the fastest growing province in Canada and in places it is also the emptiest. This is my

province and it becomes a challenge to this august body to give it good government.
During the centennial year in British Columbia, Vancouver will be the centre of many great attractions. Hon. members who visit Vancouver will find it the most exciting city in Canada from a cultural point of view; it has the potential of becoming one of the most beautiful cities on this continent.
While on this subject I would like on behalf of my constituents to suggest to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) that he give early consideration to the removal of the air force station near the Bur-rard bridge in Vancouver. This area, if transferred to a park, will add greatly to Vancouver's natural beauty. For close to 60 years the town planners and the citizens of Vancouver have dedicated this area for a park, and I am satisfied that had it not been for the war the citizens of Vancouver would now be enjoying this area as a park. I do hope the minister will give careful consideration to the Vancouver city council resolution of, I believe, October 6, 1941-passed during the war-which recorded the terms under which the air force entered this property. The war being over there is, I feel, an obligation upon this organization to move elsewhere. The recovery of this property for park purposes is as important to the city of Vancouver as was the Louisiana purchase to the United States.
May I turn now to another subject. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) in his brilliant address recently spoke of ethnic groups and of the many people who had immigrated to this country. Since the war we have received over 1| million immigrants- this is a large number-and each immigrant was accepted after having complied with the procedure laid down under the Immigration Act. It is this part of the problem which interests me most-the practice and procedure under the Immigration Act. In the movement of so many people to Canada many become bedevilled by red tape and bureaucratic snags; our immigration laws and regulations cannot, under the best of circumstances, cover all potentialities, but there is strong indication that there is much room for improvement of a large part of them in order to minimize the suffering of people who decide to come to Canada.
Years ago in Canada and in the United States the immigration policy was just a question of come one, come all. It was merely a case of moving people physically from one country to another, from say Europe to Canada.

If the immigrant was breathing upon arrival at the Canadian port he was admitted. The statue of Liberty outside New York recalls the policy of the United States in that era. Inscribed on the statue are these words:
"Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door."
During the passage of years the immigration policy of the two countries changed. New acts were drafted, new regulations formulated and new and complicated procedures adopted. It is these procedures and regulations which must now be considered. Skilled legal talent has difficulty understanding the procedural mysteries of the immigration department. Even with the best administrative radar equipment it is difficult to tell who is admissible to this country and who is not. Under the leadership of the American Bar Association the United States government amended its immigration act, its regulations and the administration thereof. The United States practitioner can now find his immigration law in legal directories such as:
"I. and N. Dec." (Administrative decisions under immigration and nationality laws of the United States); Interim Decisions, (Decisions of Board of Immigration Appeals and Central Office prior to publication in "I. and N. Dec."); "L.ed.", (Lawyers' Edition, Supreme Court Decisions) and "Op. Atty. Gen.", (Opinions of the Attorney General).
In Canada there are no such guides. Immigration cases are not reported in any journal so that no healthy body of law can be found other than the act itself. With no reporting service, there is a lack of uniformity. On the other hand, Hal Banks, with a lengthy record, is admitted to Canada while other Americans are deported with a most nominal record. Distressed immigrants or their Canadian applicants find themselves in a contest which has clearly become a struggle against bureaucracy, or to use a modern term "ministerial discretion".
With the advent of the revised act in 1953 many hoped that the evils of uncertainty and the rigid ministerial control which for so many years had plagued the field of immigration would be mitigated. Provision was made for an immigration appeal board. The sections of the old act were rearranged, additional definitions were added and the result appeared to be a better example of legislation. Unfortunately, little of substance was altered and the act together with its regulations remains as one of the saddest statutes in force today. Frustration, bewilderment and confusion have become the common lot of the person engaged in this departmental work. The administration of the act has been carried on in an atmosphere of secrecy which
The Address-Mr. Taylor has provoked sharp criticism from the bench and bar, from the press and from the general public alike.
For a generation now persons having immigration problems have approached the minister. Often these people are represented by members of the House of Commons and too often the cases are disposed of after some informal and sometimes injudicious hearing tinged, I suspect, with partisan feelings. There is no arrangement for a formal hearing. A way must be found to eliminate personal appeals to the minister at least until all remedies under the act have been exhausted. An applicant for admission either qualifies under the act or does not. An applicant should be able to test his admissibility under a proper administrative setup. If he does not qualify he is excluded, and if he does qualify he should be admitted. If there are persons who have been excluded but whose cases involve unusual and compelling circumstances, then a private bill should be applied for. In applying for a private bill all members of the house would know who was applying and what were the special circumstances.

Canadians in growing numbers will continue to condemn a policy of administration based on secrecy, refusal of reason, lack of proper tribunals to provide a full and fair hearing and the absence of any appeal procedure. There is a complete paucity of rules and regulations governing the admission procedure of dependants of Canadian citizens. If there is a hearing there is no reason why it cannot be in the presence of counsel and, unless security is in issue, there is no reason why the department cannot make available a transcript of the hearing and in due course report its decision in some journal whereby those concerned with immigration law can look to some body of law for precedents. A fair hearing and reported decisions will revolutionize the present procedure.
Canada's immigration policy under the previous Liberal administration was based on the carefully worded statement:
It is not a fundamental human right of an alien to enter Canada. It is a privilege. It is a matter of domestic policy.

The Address-Mr. Taylor
I do not necessarily disagree with this statement but I could find no statement of the previous administration as to rights or privileges of Canadians who apply for immigrants whether they be dependants, relatives or friends. It is now necessary that parliament give consideration to this aspect of the problem. The Canadian Bar Association has already studied and made recommendations in this regard. If we adopt those recommendations many of the irritating and perplexing vexations that face Canadians having immigration problems will be solved.
I have in my desk a picture taken some time ago showing British immigrants lining up by the hundreds around the Canadian immigration office in London.

That is not a comforting scene from a procedural point of view. I would like to recommend that a system and service be designed so that such immigrants would not be obliged or allowed to line up in that manner. I would also suggest that if an air bridge to Canada is to be set up again Canadian carriers be used.
The facts surrounding the Heikkila case are well known to many in Canada and to people of many other countries. Because of the treatment afforded Heikkila in Vancouver, Canada has suffered. The case smacks of the gestapo, the thumb screw and the rack. The main purpose of giving further consideration to this case is to ensure that it does not happen again.
The Heikkila case was primarily an immigration matter and it remained so until he departed from this country. It is hardly good enough for our immigration service to say to the United States escort, "We will not look after him; do what you wish with him". In this case he was taken to the police station. However, the officer could well have taken Heikkila to a local hotel and chained him to the bed. One can imagine all sorts of things happening in the event that the immigration department does not take charge of these cases.
In due course Heikkila may once again find himself in Canada. The Vancouver city officials have decided that no longer will the city jail be available to deportees. I suggest that this time he be kept in the immigration quarters at the expense of the United States government. If goods are imported into Canada, the customs department takes charge of the goods until the duty is paid or the goods vacate Canada. That department does not turn over the goods to another agency. The same principle should follow in immigration matters.

When I last spoke in this chamber I referred to a most pleasant visit to the grand province of Quebec. During the last weekend I made another visit there. My first visit to Quebec was mainly to see Maurice Richard play hockey. The last trip was to see a person in custody and now under order of deportation to Italy. I made my way to the immigration clearing centre on St. Antoine street from the beautiful new Queen Elizabeth hotel. I passed a number of fine buildings, a lovely park, fine trees and finally arrived at the immigration building which lies in the shade and gloom of the built-up marshalling yards of the Windsor station. The area, like the immigration building, is most depressive. A run-down night club and a gambling joint are close by. I have often thought that the immigration building in Vancouver was very deplorable, but it is good compared with the situation in Montreal. I would like hon. members to know that the Vancouver building is situated, as far as the eye can detect, in the freight yards of the Canadian Pacific railway. Freight trains are ever present; they shunt by day and by night. Yet this building, like the one in Montreal, incarcerates persons anywhere from a day to many months. Both buildings lack the facilities of even a third rate hotel. Here is where some of the immigrants get their first experience of Canada. The visitor to the Montreal building will see 20 persons in one room, huddled in double deck beds, where by normal standards four persons ought to be. In Montreal, as in Vancouver, immigration administration has been reduced to a third-class operation, taking its place far down the list from civic squares, city halls, express ways and clover-leafs.
I suggest, that we can do better than this, and I hope the new administration will, after it has caught its breath, give consideration to this situation. I believe we should now raise our sights and plan our immigration collection centres nearer to airports than railway stations, nearer to the country than the city, nearer to fresh air and peace and quiet than the hubbub of the city.
I believe also that Canada should encourage a stowaway law such as has been formulated in the Baltic countries. Under the proposed convention, shipowners of ratifying states would be enabled to land stowaways at the first suitable port of another ratifying state. The authorities there would return the stowaway to the state whose nationality he claimed.
In conclusion, I would like to commend the loyal and hardworking personnel of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.

They do desire to co-operate and have shown a willingness to be of service. If, of course, the rules and regulations are changed by the new administration, then I feel that they will have the opportunity of giving that type of service that they are often prevented from giving, not so much of their own volition but by the operation of the present rules and regulations. I have come to know many fine officers in the department, men of remarkable stature. Mr. A. L. Jolliffe, now retired would be in that class, but there are others who are also now serving. In passing I would like to pay tribute to my father, who like the rest, made a mistake here or there, but wherever possible emphasized the humanities ahead of the regulations.

Mr. Speaker, man is subject to the influences of environment and as I rise to speak in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne this is a moment that I will long remember. I can assure you that I share the same reactions of nervousness, timidity and humbleness that no doubt many of my predecessors have felt in rising to address the House of Commons for the first time.
Before I continue, Mr. Speaker, allow me to add my congratulations to you, the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees. I am quite certain that the high responsibilities you have been called upon to perform will be carried out in the highest

traditions of this house. I would like also to add my congratulations to my friends, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) and the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who so capably moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I might say in passing that the principles envisioned by the speaker from the Yukon outline something that is very near and dear to the hearts of the people of Saskatchewan. As you know, for years we have been more or less depending on bread alone but with the development of our great northland I feel we will not remain in the category of hewers of wood and drawers of water. I see the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) on the other side of the house and I can assure him on behalf of myself and my colleagues that we will be solidly behind him in the pursuit of his duties along this line.
For a few moments, I would like to say something about the great constituency of Moose Mountain which I have the honour to represent in the house. When I use the word "great" in referring to my constituency it means that I have always thought a great deal of that area of Canada because I was born there and because of the fine people who reside there, but since March 31 I am even more appreciative because on that day I was elected to represent Moose Mountain as the first Conservative member of parliament since confederation. I can assure you that if I have my way, and with the aid of the good government policies being laid down by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his many colleagues in the next few months, I will not, I hope, be the last Conservative elected from Moose Mountain.
Geographically my constituency is located in the extreme southeast corner of Saskatchewan and is one of three long rectangular shaped constituencies whose area stretches the whole breadth of Saskatchewan. Its southern boundary commences in the southeast corner of Saskatchewan and follows the United States border due west approximately 110 miles, then goes due north about 60 miles, then directly east again for 110 miles and then due south along the Manitoba boundary to the starting point. Within its boundaries is a population of 45,000 people living on farms, in 79 towns, villages, and hamlets, and one city, Estevan, our largest urban centre of 8,000 people.
Basically agriculture is our chief industry but we also have a large soft or lignite coal mining industry situated at Bienfait and Estevan which provides employment for several thousand people. This coal area is one 57071-3-42J
The Address-Mr. Southam of the largest in western Canada. There has been a change over the past few years from deep seam mining to surface mining and recently it has been a very interesting sight to see some of the largest dragline shovels on the North American continent biting out great gobs of coal weighing up to 25 tons, the clay having first been taken off the surface and piled up in huge mounds. This available source of coal provides cheap fuel for a large part of Saskatchewan and is shipped as far east as Winnipeg, Manitoba, where large quantities are used, especially in the stoker size.
Another fast developing and important industry is oil. Large and valuable finds have recently been made in this part of Saskatchewan and development in a number of areas has recently taken place. Estevan is the centre of activity of the oil business but many other and lucrative fields include Good-water, Midale, Frobisher, Oxbow, Alida, Carnduff and Nottingham. To cite an example of one small area, Steelman at the present time has well over 300 producing wells. Unfortunately for the individual, most of the oil rights are held by the crown. However, quite a few early settlers or their descendants, especially in the eastern part of Moose Mountain, held their mineral rights and in some cases where they did not dispose of them or lease too early they have greatly enhanced their economy through the recent development that has taken place there.
The Saskatchewan Power Corporation is presently building a $40 million power development project known as the Boundary dam, four miles south of Estevan. This plant, designed on the steam turbo basis, will utilize about 100,000 tons of soft coal per year and the resulting power production will not only be a great asset to Saskatchewan in the near future but could quite conceivably lead to a chemical industry being established in that area because of the ready availability of oil and gas by-products.
In so far as our farm economy is concerned, it is mostly on a mixed farming basis with considerable wasteland being utilized by some fine cattle herds and a number of hogs being raised. There has been a trend away from dairy herds during the past few years, but the recent decline in farm income has caused people to again take a look at this side of the farm prospects. Wheat is by far the largest grain product, with flax, oats and barley being extensively grown, as well as some corn and grass seed. Poultry has been in low production, but recently a few farmers have established large turkey flocks which have proven to be a reasonably good addition to their economy.

The Address-Mr. Southam
In considering the general economic situation of the western farmer I should like to say that the farmers in my constituency were pleased to learn of the Conservative government's awareness of their problems last fall when they immediately set about introducing legislation making available interest-free cash advances on farm-stored grain. Although this was not a cure-all by any means, it did make some ready cash available when it was needed most.
The most far-reaching, positive, and practical piece of farm legislation ever passed was Bill No. 237, the price stabilization act. I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the members of his cabinet and the advisory board upon this magnificent achievement. Despite the sometimes slanderous and derogatory remarks, as well as the stiff opposition put up for purely selfish political motives by one of the small opposition groups, the bill was passed and I think the electors' reaction to this legislation was clearly demonstrated on March 31.
I was very happy the other morning to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) say, in answer to a question, that the government was seriously considering the question of deficiency payments on western grain. Regardless of how effective the farm stabilization act may be, it still does not cover the western producer's basic commodity, wheat. A recent study made by the Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba wheat pools, a group that handles the biggest share of western grain, has brought to light some very practical figures which clearly show the need for some additional assistance. I should like your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, to read into the record the details of the case put up by the western wheat pools.
I would suggest in passing that should a deficiency payment plan be established by the government it should cover the two years 1955-56 and 1956-57. In other words, two moderate payments made retroactive for the two years mentioned would be better than one larger payment made for one year. I suggest this because Saskatchewan has such a large geographical area that in one section we find that in a certain year good yields were received, while in another section poor yields were received in the same year. If the deficiency payments were smaller but covered the two years it would be of the most benefit to the most people.
The case for deficiency payments as set forth by the wheat pools is as follows:
The plan for deficiency payments on wheat, oats and barley delivered to the Canadian Wheat Board for the seasons 1955-56 and 1956-57 proposed by the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta wheat pools

is based on the submission made to the government by the three prairie wheat pools on January 13, 1958.
It should be noted that the basis for determining the level of deficiency payments is related to Saskatchewan farm prices. It is assumed that if the plan is implemented, Canadian Wheat Board figures for the three prairie provinces will be used instead of Saskatchewan figures. Preliminary checking indicates that the figure for the three provinces would be approximately the same as for Saskatchewan.
The case for deficiency payments is based on some of the following factors:
(a)	Since 1947 there has been an increase of 50.3 per cent in the cost of goods and services used by farmers.
(b)	During the same period there has been a 20.8 per cent drop in the average price of wheat on the farm. The average price for barley has dropped 27 per cent and oats have dropped 36.7 per cent.
(c)	Only once in the history of western Canadian agriculture has the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat been lower than it is now, and that was in the great depression of the 1930's.
(d)	It took one box carload of grain to buy a small combine in 1946. Now it takes 2] carloads. (1,845 bushels compared with 3,963 bushels).
(e)	The farm income problem is not directly related to lack of markets. The average annual deliveries from the farm for the last five years amounted to 391 million bushels. The 35-year average was 319 million bushels.
(f)	Average exports of wheat for the last five years amounted to 292 million of wheat annually compared with an average of 257 million bushels annually for the past 35 years.
While these developments have been occurring which adversely affect the position of the farmer, other segments of the economy have been able to offset increase in costs:
(a)	Since 1947 the average weekly earnings of those employed in industry exclusive of the primary production industries have increased by 77.3 per cent.
(b)	The gross national product which may be regarded as the barometer of economic activity has more than doubled.
(c)	The general wholesale price index has risen 39.5 per cent.
(d)	General freight rates have increased by about 116 per cent.
The case for deficiency payments is based on the principle that grain producers should receive a return from the production of the farm that will bear a fair relationship to their costs of production and to Canadian living standards.
This was submitted on April 30, 1958 by the Manitoba pool elevators, the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Alberta wheat pool. I would suggest that these grain marketing agencies represent about 185,000 of our farm population.
In the light of the Baker commission report which indicates a complete agrarian change is taking place, especially in Saskatchewan, I strongly urge that if a deficiency payment is made, and I seriously feel it should be, we have a ceiling placed on whatever payment formula may be set up. Once a level of payments has been approved, the machinery of the Canadian wheat board could be used to

determine the exact amount of money involved and also make the distribution. "
Another serious problem we have in western Canada, as was pointed out in the Baker commission report, concerns the exodus of the young farmer from his normal farm environment to the larger urban centres. In so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, quite often he has moved right out of the province. The result of this has been that Saskatchewan over the last 10 years has shown a decrease in population compared to the large increases in other provinces. In order to rectify this situation I should like to endorse some plan that would make available to bona fide young farmers, and those in the middle age groups who wanted to increase their holdings, a long-term low-interest rate loan. This is something that is badly needed and is long overdue.
Another suggestion I should like to make, now that the federal government is taking over responsibility for helping to eradicate brucellosis in cattle, is that this policy be speeded up. Some teeth should be put in the act apparently because there seems to be some laxity in the application of the law applying to this disease, with resultant heavy losses in cattle herds in some parts of Saskatchewan.
I should like to say that after listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith) on May 22, I heartily concur with his remarks pertaining to education. I have always maintained that the best asset a country has is the people who live in that country. It is a government's basic responsibility, therefore, to see that all the people have the opportunity of having a healthy body and an informed mind. These two things, tempered with some Christian education by their parents and churches, will give us the type of Canadian citizen about whom posterity will not have to be too much concerned.
In so far as health services are concerned, I should like to suggest that the government should give early consideration to a plan for the payment of depreciation costs on buildings and equipment, in conjunction with the program for building new hospitals.
Since the history-making events of March 31 I have heard quite a number of opposition groups express concern over the fact that the Prime Minister and his Conservative group have such a large majority in this house. I would hasten to say that since I come from Saskatchewan it has been my privilege to know the Prime Minister for some considerable period of time, and I can assure those who may be concerned that this large majority will only provide an extra incentive for him to work harder in
The Address-Mr. Drouin co-operation with his colleagues to implement the far-reaching policies of our party, rather than to take advantage of this situation about which they are worried. As proof of this contention I would cite the fact that the Prime Minister has presented, through the speech from the throne, the most far-reaching, positive and practical legislative program that this house has had the opportunity of debating in many years. Another indication of the fact the government does not intend to take undue advantage of its numerical superiority is the fact that they invited the opposition to appoint one of their members to be chairman of the committee of supply. This is the first time this has been done in the history of our parliament, and it is a very significant and most democratic gesture.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that as a member of this government I feel it is our responsibility to see to it that all citizens living within the boundaries of this great land of ours should have an equal opportunity.
In working towards this end in co-operation with my colleagues, I feel I shall be accomplishing the most for my constituency in particular, and Canada as a whole, and that we can all join in looking forward to this second half of the twentieth century as the dawn of a bright new era in Canada, this place we call our home.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasant duty, moved by feelings of the sincerest and deepest gratitude, to thank the electors of Dorchester most gratefully for the confidence they expressed in me on the elections of March 31 last. They can all rest assured of my entire devotion so that we may avail ourselves of the benefits of an efficient administration.
On my constituents' behalf, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate you for the confidence which the house has once more placed in you in re-appointing you as its Speaker.
My congratulations also go to the members for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) and for Spa-dina (Mr. Rea) who were respectively chosen chairman and deputy chairman of committees of the whole. The hon. members for Lotbiniere (Mr. O'Hurley) and for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) have received portfolios. We trust that, with their experience and their innate sense of devotion to their work, they will co-operate with their cabinet colleagues in solving the problems which beset Canadians at this time.

The Address-Mr. Drouin
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the magnificent way in which they have acquitted themselves of their task.
I thank my constituents for providing me with this opportunity of sitting in the Canadian parliament, following in the footsteps of the great men who have already represented the constituency of Dorchester and whose names are inscribed in the golden book of the province of Quebec. I refer to the hon. member who represented the constituency of Dorchester in 1911 and whose son honours at this time the House of Commons as its Deputy Speaker. I refer also to the first citizen of the province of Quebec, the present lieutenant governor who sat here for Dorchester between 1930 and 1935.
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Dorchester is a fine constituency situated on the southern shore of the St. Lawrence, whose landscape is graced by several rivers flowing against the background of the Appalachian mountains.
As neighbours I have the pleasure of having to the north, a great lawyer, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion), to the west, the hon. member for Lotbiniere, the Minister of Defence Production, to the east, our good friends the Americans and to the south, the hon. member for Beauce, Mr. Racine, to whom I would like to wish a very happy stay in this house. I do hope that he will receive the gift of wisdom, so that he may rest at peace with himself during the four next years of the life of this parliament.
Mr. Speaker, my constituents live by agriculture, lumbering, maple syrup production and some local trade. I would like to point out to the house that even if the constituency of Dorchester is beautiful to the point of engaging a poet's fancy, it is nevertheless an extremely poor area since it has always been neglected and since its geographical location makes it impossible for it to benefit from large scale public works as has been the case in other constituencies.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government which was in power for 22 years was never too liberal with the constituency of Dorchester. There is not a single breathing soul who could, at this time, in the constituency of Dorchester, bear witness to the existence of that government. And yet in 1957 and 1958 we heard our hon. friends to the right singing the praises and extolling the virtues of the Liberal government. Oh! it was something, Mr. Speaker, to hear those descriptions


of Liberal government achievements! We were given to understand, or at least such was my impression, that it was a highly precise mechanism, a masterpiece made by certain highly trained specialists who had managed to set up a kind of fascinating scientific instrument. We were told that the country was prosperous, that taxes could not be lowered, that agriculture was in a wonderful position-according to the hon. member of Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) -and that moreover, the Liberal government had had the wisdom to name wise men to look after Canada's interests abroad.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, a few months with a government bent on saving Canada for Canadians were enough to show decisively that the theories of the last government were wrong. Taxes were reduced and Canadians breathe easier. The present agricultural legislation is worthy of the wisdom of a Solomon. In the haven of peace, vigilant lookouts stand on guard to prevent a recurrence of past catastrophes.
Mr. Speaker, it seems inconceivable that the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) should claim that the Conservative government has always brought depression to our country; uncontrovertible facts prove the contrary. In 1929, under a Liberal government there was a memorable market crash which plunged the whole country headlong into a baleful depression. In 1930, the economic depression sank to even greater depths. For five years, the Conservative government did its best to correct the mistakes of the Liberal government. In 1935, the Liberal government was back in the saddle on the strength of statements that no other party could pull the country out of the depression. Yet, conditions remained just as hard and deplorable, and the number of unemployed reached astronomical proportions, up to 1939. In 1956, the Liberal government's carelessness touched off a new economic depression.
Mr. Speaker, I resent the snide remarks of my friends over here who claim there is a definite difference between the members from the province of Quebec and those from the rest of the country. To a certain extent, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. members of the opposition. It is indeed true that they themselves consistently strive to tear pieces out of the most sacred document we have in this country, the British North America Act, a document responsible for the unity, the enlightenment and the peace of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to thank the government and its leader for the excellent legislation enacted since they came to power.
Allow me also to draw the attention of that same government to the urgent needs of the constituency of Dorchester. We are well located geographically and there would be room in my riding for heavy industry. It would make up for the mistake of the former government which put all its eggs in one basket or, in other words, concentrated the whole industry of Canada in a rather restricted area, a very unhappy situation from a strategic point of view.
It seems to me that the people of eastern Canada also pay taxes. We are big buyers, and as far as industry is concerned, we are not getting our fair share. Every day we witness the breakdown of families whose children have to seek work in factories abroad, manufacturing the plough that will be used in tilling the ancestral land.
I should like to urge upon the government the processing of our raw materials here in Canada and specially not to export raw steel from the province of Quebec because, at the same time, we export employment.
I would also ask the government to impose severe penalties on companies who exploited our farmers in the purchase of pulpwood, especially in the constituency of Dorchester.
May I also ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to restore the subsidy on aluminum buckets for maple syrup, which subsidy was abolished by the Liberal government in 1954.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to have a look at the public works started way back in 1933 by the Conservative government, in the constituency of Dorchester, and which was left unfinished, like Schubert's symphony. The Liberal government never had the courage to complete the public works started from 1930 to 1935 by my illustrious predecessor.
I would also like to remind the government with particular emphasis of the greatest weatth of our country, a wealth greater than all our mines, greater than all the wheat of our western prairies, namely, our young people. It seems to me that it is our urgent duty and absolute obligation to invest money in an asset so rich, so promising, that nothing else in this country can pay higher dividends.
In my opinion, if family allowances were doubled, it would be easier to open to these young folk the doors of our schools and of
The Address-Mr. Yacula our universities. There would be less juvenile delinquency, fewer prisons and, on the other hand, more teachers and more scientists.
Mr. Speaker, I submit those few remarks to the government and to its enlightened leader, hoping to see them acted upon.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express in this house, on my own behalf and on behalf of my constituents, the confidence we have in our right honourable leader. We know that he is in the same class with the Macdonalds, the Bennetts, and so on. We know that he will bring the light of day to our country. We know that he is a great star, shining over Canada, enlightening it and making it a better country to live in.

To the group of eight may I quote the

The Address-Mr. Yacula words of Professor John Jewkes of Oxford, as reported in the Reader's Digest of June, 1953, as follows:
On my recent trip to the U.S.A., I have found an uncomfortable feeling that something is happening in American society which is familiar to me because it happened in Great Britain.
There seem to be in American colleges these days many teachers who speak of the virtues of a centrally planned economy with the starry-eyed enthusiasm and the almost touching innocence regarding the realities of economic life which were so apparent in British universities between the wars. There seems to be a growing contempt for profit making, a growing irritability with the pains of readjustment which a system of free enterprise makes inevitable as, in the course of progress, it continually bursts out of its skin to take a new form. And I begin to ask myself: Is it conceivable that the American people, having provided so strong a proof of the virtues of a free economy, are gradually becoming unaware of, or indifferent to, the secrets of their own greatness?

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock I was saying that during the election campaign the Liberals were laying all the blame for the ills of this country on the Conservative party but let me now quote what the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) said in an article published in the January 1958 issue of Fortune magazine when a number of thinking people were asked to name the most important economic problem confronting the United States in the next 20 years. You will note that the recession is not mentioned by the hon. member. He said, in part:
The most important economic problem facing the United States economy during the next 20 years will be that arising from its growing reluctance to rely on international specialization and trade.
If this becomes a fixed and permanent policy, then other countries will inevitably draw the conclusion that the United States is not going to accept its responsibilities as the world's leading creditor nation by the adoption of appropriate trade policies.
Such a conclusion can be reached in spite of the amazing generosity of the American people- unparalleled in history-in their aid program for less fortunate nations.
What, however, is required is trade, not aid, and this means changes in United States policy. Without such changes there will be economic conflict, rather than economic co-operation, between the
[Mr. Yacula. 1
United States and its friends. And without economic co-operation it will be increasingly difficult to work together politically and for collective defence.
The final decision rests with United States firms themselves. They should agree to invest more capital abroad in the form of loans and bonds and less in the form of equity capital.
They should be content with less ownership and control in other countries.
In such an event without forfeiting the legitimate reward which they have a right to expect for their efforts, they will avoid those undesirable political repercussions in the economic field which can have unhappy political consequences.
And again, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 22,
The hon. member for Algoma East was one of the few voices coming out strongly to say that American protectionism is damaging western unity. Why is it, he asked, that Americans are prepared to spend large sums to aid other countries but will do little trading with them? He said that Americans will take action to protect a single group in the United States of America without considering that this action might mean "disaster for another country which is a friend of yours."
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in regard to my constituency of Springfield, one of the largest in Canada, embracing an area roughly speaking west of the historic Red river from Emesville and Rossdale to the Ontario boundary line and south from the new No. 1 highway north to Berens river.
We Canadians are proud to possess two of the greatest assets:	one, our natural
resources without which no country can contribute freely either to its citizens or to the world at large, and the other our population which is the greatest asset any country can possess. Canada is proud to have within her realm a population made up of various backgrounds, a veritable mosaic indeed. A pot containing the best soup in the world. Look within the walls of this parliament and you will see representatives of various colours, races and religions representing different sections of this country. One such section among the 265 is my constituency of Springfield which today I have the honour and good fortune to represent in this great parliament of Canada, a parliament which does and will continue to play an important part in the affairs of this country and outside of Canada as [DOT] well. Our two greatest assets are, then, our natural resources and our people.
My constituency is rich in natural resources but these must be developed by means of governmental direction and vision. At the extreme north of my constituency are deposits of great mineral wealth as witness the San Antonio mines. But these resources need roads to get to them and bridges over which to cross the waters. In the town of Bissett is

an industry giving employment and developing another fine community of splendid men, women and children but they need our praise and encouragement.
Travelling south from Bissett we come to Pine Falls where a large paper mill is in operation giving employment to hundreds of farmers, wood cutters, truckers, transportation agencies, et cetera. Pine Falls is a beautiful town indeed and a great asset, not only to my constituency but to the growth and development of the province of Manitoba and Canada as a whole. But up to now this great industrial town has not had a decent road and it is roads that create and establish friendship, neighbourliness and unity in any district.
In that same area we have a great historical river rushing into lake Winnipeg. On that river within my constituency are five power plants, the Pine Falls plant, the Great falls plant, the MacArthur falls plant, the Pointe du Bois plant and the Seven Sisters falls plant supplying power to Winnipeg and the surrounding districts. These areas also have great scenic beauty and are important tourist attractions but we, as Canadians, lack the initiative, courage and vision to build roads into these areas in order to transform these century-old -if I may use the term-sedentary resources into human usefulness and reality. I trust that when my government undertakes its great national development scheme the term "north" will include the northern area of my constituency.
I have other things to relate about my constituency. In the village of Whitemouth there is a fine brickyard and in Julius, a moss plant that has been giving employment to farmers in their spare time enabling them to earn much needed dollars. This plant makes use of our marshes and swamps which for centuries were characterized as useless in the production of valuable and necessary products. But this enterprise has had very little encouragement from outside sources and worst of all it too needs roads which could be maintained by the industry. In fact, there is no sign on the highway to attract the attention of tourists.
One of our major municipalities, St. Clements, has the Canadian Industries Limited plant and a power plant is under construction. Lac du Bonnet has a rice processing and alfalfa plant. The Brokenhead municipality is noted for Garson and Tyndall stones. You will find that the walls of this parliament building are built of Tyndall stone. Other areas are noted for mixed farming. Gonor and Narol-the latter one of the largest villages in Canada-are especially famous for market gardening. Beausejour is, as it were,
The Address-Mr. Yacula the capital of my constituency. It is a town with electricity, sewer and water, a hospital, recreational and educational facilities, hotel accommodation and a most attractive area for new industrial establishments. Here is located one of the largest farm markets in eastern Manitoba, an excellent place for buyers and sellers to meet. Lockport is a great recreational centre but the bridge there needs widening to permit an ever-increasing number of cars to pass over it. It is a veritable bottleneck now.
In referring to my constituency I cannot neglect mentioning what is being done for the Lac du Bonnet district, for my constituency, for Manitoba, for Canada and perhaps for the North American continent by a gentleman named Mr. Fred Gauer who is in the process of building and establishing one of the largest turkey farms in the world. The establishment will consist of modern, up to date buildings of fireproof and steel construction. Turkeys there will live an ideal turkey life. The farm and processing plant will be capable of processing 250,000 turkeys. This will, indeed, help Lac du Bonnet and Mr. Gauer is indeed doing his share as a great Canadian in promoting industry and giving employment to a number of people in the constituency of Springfield.
But do we appreciate as administrators of government what he is doing for us? Not too much. He needs a road able to handle the heavy traffic necessary over which to deliver supplies of feed stores, oil, et cetera. This is where good government should come in. Why have I mentioned these things? It is because we as a government should encourage and help to make these industries bigger and happier so that they may go on expanding and hiring more people and thus go on building larger and better up to date communities.
The population of this country is one of our greatest assets. Our boys and girls must have food, clothing and shelter, but these must be provided by their parents and the parents must have work. This work must be provided by individuals and private industries or establishments and the whole panorama of activities must be looked after or supervised by the government. In this way the whole circle of our economy will run efficiently. I say that when we can wage wars successfully we ought to be able to fight recessions and depressions just as successfully and effectively, in fact more so. For wars destroy and things destroyed must be replaced, but during times of peace we do not destroy, we create.
Food, clothing and shelter in fair abundance will eliminate and eradicate communism
658	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Yacula and unrest but starvation, rags and slums are hotbeds for the dissemination of reactionary ideas. I, therefore, suggest that the government go full steam ahead into the things we promised our people to do, to bring about better times, better fortunes and above all, a bigger Canada.
Realizing that the new and young are always ready to give those who are older than themselves the full benefit of their inexperience, may I suggest that we look ahead and try to win the battle which is going to confront us. Let us not believe in the policy that it is the survival of the slickest, rather let us believe that it is the survival of the best and the fittest. Who is the fittest? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, it is the present government! The present Progressive Conservative ' party is a purely Canadian party. It was born on June 10, 1957 and it will be a robust one-year old Canadian on June 10, 1958. This one year old Canadian will be able to stand up for serenity, sympathy, simplicity, sincerity and security.
This one year old has passed the farm bill No. 237 which will provide a flexible price support program to provide stabilization of prices of agricultural commodities. Action was taken to protect our pea growers and poultry farmers. Action was also taken to set or extend price supports on butter and butterfat, sugar beets and eggs. More money was set aside with which to build new houses and unemployment benefits were extended recently. These are just a few of the things that this government did. And why Mr. Speaker? Because we have a great Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). In the Prime Minister we have a man of dynamic personality, a man of generous thought, a man of sincerity, a man of vision, a man of faith, a unifier. The Prime Minister has united this country again. In passing, may I say he has even united the Ukrainians. Whereas previously their representation in parliament consisted of one Conservative, one Liberal, one C.C.F.'er and one Social Crediter, today there are six and they are all Conservatives.
I am for a great national public works undertaking. It is roads that cement us together. It was the C.P.R. that saved Canada and united her from coast to coast. It was Sir John A. Macdonald, who without the present availability of capital and skill, equipment and population, sir, went ahead and achieved the magnificent feat of laying steel from one sea to another in a period of ten years.
And yet during the 23 years of Liberal regime, with all the easy availability of capital, engineering skill, tools of precision and heavy machinery, what have they built


in the way of a national highway? The trans-Canada has been under construction for years and what have they done? They merely patched and patched and patched. They built a patch-quilt, a trail. Have we in western Canada seen cars from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec? Is Canada, whose population will soon reach the 20 million mark, going to be satisfied with a No. 1 highway? And why, sir? Because the Liberals lacked faith and vision. Even today they think of Canada in terms of igloos and wigwams.
It was this dilly-dallying, indecision and lack of vision that cost the ratepayers of this country millions of dollars extra. I refer to the Winnipeg post office. Had this been built years ago it would have cost this country $3 million instead of $9 million. I say that that is why we became regionalized and sectionalized, if I may use these words, during the late Liberal government.
Before concluding I would suggest that the government give consideration to the possibility of trading with Russia and China. Here are two important countries, ready to do business with us. The recent visit of Canadian businessmen to Russia strongly suggests such an undertaking. Since Russia has risen from a peasant state to one comparable with any of the modern powers in the field of culture, sports et cetera and since Russia is here to stay we should be able to co-exist with her. Diplomatically we have accomplished that; politically we have not.
Let me quote from a submission to the Canadian government on May 28, 1958, by the interprovincial farm union council. At page 7 we find this:
Anything that will encourage development in Canada, increase the population and keep the general economy at a high level is beneficial to agriculture. There is no better market than our home market, but international trade is also of great importance to Canadian agriculture. Anything that can be done to encourage international trade will work to the benefit of agriculture and will enable us to sell more of our products on the world market. In the light of the current general economic situation, it is imperative that we re-assess our national trade policies.
I shall conclude by saying, first, that the throne speech is an excellent document of action, and is certainly superior in both quantity and quality to the one read on January 8, 1957. Secondly, I wish to thank the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) for giving the members of this house the opportunity to become acquainted with the activities and establishments under his jurisdiction. The visit to Kingston on May 24 was a great success, and the courtesy shown throughout the tour by all concerned was beyond description.

That is something that is so often forgotten. My hon. friends opposite think that Canadian history began on June 10, 1957. I am quite ready to confess, Mr. Speaker, that a new chapter of Canadian history began on June 10, 1957 but we are not very confident that the things that will be written in that chapter will be as greatly to the advantage of our country as those that were written in the chapter which preceded.
There was something else we on this side of the house proposed during the election campaign, and this is another idea which is given without any requirement of acknowledgment by my hon. friends opposite. It has been pointed out already by this side in the short debate we had the other day on housing problems that there is an urgent need to speed up the redevelopment of blighted areas in our cities. In order to promote this redevelopment program we proposed if we were in a position of responsibility to do it to amend the existing legislation to provide for greater participation by the federal government in this activity. In particular, we proposed to increase federal participation in slum clearance schemes from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and to provide for federal sharing in the cost of water, sewer and street services in the area concerned. Also we proposed to ease the present restrictions on redevelopment so as to permit redevelopment for commercial and other purposes as well as for housing if that were considered advisable.

So when I say that we on this side support an amendment which advocates legislation to ease the burden on municipalities we at the same time make concrete proposals to that end.
In a few minutes, we will be voting on the address. As I have said, we will vote in favour of the address but I also want to remove any possibility of any misunderstanding as to the significance of that vote. The motion that we will vote on is merely this:
That the following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency the Right Honourable Vincent Massey, Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour, Governor General and Commander-inChief of Canada.
May it please Your Excellency:
We, Her Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both houses of parliament.
In other words, this is simply a word of thanks and appreciation to His Excellency for the speech addressed to both houses at the opening of parliament. It is nothing more and nothing less than that. It follows the traditional pattern in that regard and the vote, of course, will follow that traditional pattern. Perhaps hon. members, especially the new members, may be interested in learning that in 1946 there was an explanation by the prime minister of that day, Mr. Mackenzie King, as to the significance of this kind of vote at this time. In that explanation Mr. King quoted from a work by Todd on parliamentary government, and I read from page 354 of Hansard for March 28, 1946. He said:
It has now become a well-established rule, to regard the speech from the throne, and the address in reply thereto, as reciprocal acts of courtesy between the crown and the houses of parliament, and the address itself as the unanimous and respectful expression of the deference with which the house should leceive the first communication of the session from the sovereign, and as pledging the house to nothing, save the serious consideration of the matters referred to therein.
Again from that work, Mr. King quoted the following:
Accordingly, it has gradually become the practice to refrain from moving an amendment to the address in answer to the royal speech, "unless some great political objects were in view, and likely to be attained"; or, unless some assertion were made in the address to which the opposition found it impossible to assent.
We have moved our amendments, Mr. Speaker, and when those amendments are disposed of one way or the other, then there remains the vote on the address in accordance with the custom and convention laid down in the words I have just read. In the course of

his remarks in 1946, Mr. King was interrupted by the leader of the C.C.F. party, Mr. Cold-well, who said:
May I ask the Prime Minister a question? Does he then regard the passage of the address, without division, as an expression of confidence in the government?
Mr. Mackenzie King, who was prime minister and not leader of the opposition at that time, said:
Most certainly not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the whole point.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to make that clear. Nor does the passage of the address without division commit any member to anything expressed in the address. An amendment affords an opportunity to take exception to what appears or does not appear in the speech from the throne and to the government's policy, but when amendments which have been proposed are rejected and there is nothing left but the simple expression of thanks to His Majesty or His Majesty's representative for having come to parliament and opened its proceedings, it certainly places the Commons in an anomalous position vis-a-vis the crown to refuse to thank His Majesty or His Majesty's representative for that act of courtesy.
Mr. Speaker, we in the loyal opposition do not wish to be placed in that anomalous and disloyal position, and for that reason, and for that reason only, we will support the address.

The meeting which I hope will be convened with representatives of the association of Canadian mayors cannot take place until after the commonwealth conference which is fixed for September. As soon thereafter as it is possible to do so the municipalities of this country are going to be given the opportunity to place their views before the government, and before the people of Canada, to the end that we shall be able to do something factually to meet a problem, complex in its amplitude, difficult as it is, which will provide them with further opportunities to carry out their constitutional responsibilities.
I realize that during the period from 1935 to 1957 the municipalities have year by year found themselves caught in a position which is detrimental to the discharge by them of their responsibilities under law. In that period of time the municipal share of the taxation dollar has continued to diminish to a point where there is need for some action to be taken to meet the very great challenge that faces municipalities in the discharge of their responsibilities.
I simply rose for the purpose of referring to the amendment and also to say a word to my hon. friend in appreciation of the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l	1

solicitude that he now has for the municipalities of this country which during the period of office of the late government were the forgotten bodies in this country. I say that we have given an example of facing the issue, as we did in January last in the extra assistance given to the various provinces, and thereby indirectly to the municipalities. This is evidence of our desire to assure them a degree of fairness, justice and equity which will in the years ahead characterize the relations of the country as a whole to the municipalities.
I do not fail to remember that when we brought in the legislation to give extra assistance to the maritime provinces, $7,500,000 to three of the provinces and $2,500,000 to Prince Edward Island by agreement and the additional amounts provided by changing the taxation basis from 10 per cent to 13 per cent, my hon. friends opnosite said those things would not be appreciated; they were practically of no importance. I found that wherever I went in this country there was a new attitude, a new realization on the part of the people that this government intended and will continue to carry out its promises to the end that this confederation will be assured of the strongest possible fiscal relations in so far as the provinces and municipalities are concerned. We wish to bring about the achievement of a new development policy, which is the aspiration and desire of the members of this government, the members supporting this government and I think generally the Canadian people.

I have been looking them over very carefully, and Mr. St. Laurent who was then in the house and who, in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), spoke first after the motion was introduced, welcomed this increase and welcomed the fact that it was based precisely on the formula that Mr. Harris and Mr. St. Laurent had devised. And, sir, if that 10 per cent increase, which was a substantial increase, that $62 million added to the $631 million that went to the provinces under the Liberal legislation, was helpful to the municipalities, surely the original $631 million was also helpful to the same end.
The view which Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Harris and every speaker for the Liberal government took over the period was precisely the view that the right hon. gentleman has now learned since he came into office, namely that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces. When the Prime Minister was over here he did what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) did not make the mistake of doing tonight. When he was over here he talked as though the federal government could enter into direct relations with the municipalities in these matters.

speechtext:
He soon discovered that was not possible. All he has been able to salvage out of his promises in the 1957 election campaign is an informal conference with the mayors and municipalities, exactly like those that have been held ever since 1945. That is all the Prime Minister's speech amounts to. The fact of the matter is, if my memory serves me, that there was less than $100 million paid in 1945 to the nine provinces under the federal-provincial arrangements then in force. When we went out of office it was $631 million. It is true there were ten provinces at that time, but there was well over $600 million for the nine. It had been multiplied by more than six times in the period since the war.
When hon. gentlemen who used to sit over here talked about the unfair division of the tax dollar they never took into account the very large sums which were collected by the federal treasury and paid out under the tax rental agreements and which most of the provinces in turn shared with the municipalities. That has been the way, the classic way, the right way, to aid municipalities, and I was very pleased to hear the right hon.
The Address-Mr. Kucherepa gentleman tonight admit that it was the only effective way of doing it. In so saying he was paying a very high compliment indeed to the government which had devised those relationships.
If these relationships, which were so unsatisfactory to a few hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec and were the cause of protests on their part when they were over here on this side of the house, are now supported by them when they are in the government, I think we can be grateful for this great act of unification. I remember what the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Mac-donnell), said yesterday about national unity. If the Conservative victory is going to have the effect of making it possible for the people of Quebec and especially for the government of Quebec to accept these sensible arrangements for the division of revenues between the federal and provincial governments which have meant so much to the progress of this country and the municipalities in the ten years or more since the war, if they are now going to be accepted all over the country, perhaps that is not too high a price to have paid for the government we now have.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker of the House of Commons. I should like also to take this opportunity to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the magnificent victory he won as leader of the Progressive Conservative party on March 31 last. I sincerely hope, as I am sure all hon. members do, that he will long retain his strength and health and that he may be able to give our country that kind of leadership for which he has already become renowned.
The last speaker, the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), made mention of the question of national unity. Much has already been said on this question during this parliament and the last one, and I should like to reiterate words I uttered in this connection in the house on November 12 last. At that time I said, as found on page 1008 of Hansard:
I think most hon. members have heard on countless occasions exalted speakers of the Liberal party
668	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Kucherepa
announce and reiterate the achievements of national unity amongst the people of Canada, which they claimed were built on rugged foundations which would forever hold. Now that the Liberal party has suffered a defeat at the polls It seems that in the opinion of some of the hon. members of that party this means the end of national unity in our country. If anything, I would say those revealing and startling remarks made by some of the hon. members opposite merely serve to underline the fact that the Conservative party which now forms the government has, as those speaking the truth always will, emerged as a great Canadian party which represents all the provinces and all the groups which constitute this great Canada of ours.
I want to say that our party by virtue of its composition, built as it is on this broad national foundation and having as it does representatives from not only the two great ethnic groups of which some hon. members have spoken but also from other important groups, ethnic and otherwise, will jealously guard the rights of all minorities, big or small, notwithstanding the fact that a particular group may, on occasion, and for quite plausible reasons, support more strongly some other party.
I do not think there is anything remarkable in this regard about the results of the June 10 election. Nine of our ten provinces contributed most of the increase in the number of seats held by the Conservative party in the House of Commons. The people of Canada wanted to change their government, and they voted for a Conservative administration. In so far as the people of Quebec are concerned they did what I consider to be rather a common thing in free elections; they supported what is known in political parlance as "their favourite son", a man who is a great Canadian and who has always commanded a great deal of personal support in his home province, even as some other outstanding hon. members of this house, past and present, have commanded support in other years and in other parts of the country. That man, of course, is the right hon Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent).
I believe this is a common condition existing not only in Canada but in other democracies. What *	*s unfortunate for the members opposite
is that right now, at least, there is not one among them who could possibly emulate that distinguished Canadian of whom I have just spoken. Therefore I have every confidence that when the opportunity presents itself the good people of the province of Quebec will join the people of the other nine provinces in supporting, in equal measure, the Conservative party which is today the living symbol of national unity.
